articles.s: JERRABOMBERRA, Australia — November 10, 2026 — lululemon is launching a limited capsule in Australia and New Zealand featuring two core run styles made with enzymatically recycled polyester. Developed through its long-term work with Australian-based Samsara Eco, the capsule’s Hotty Hot High-Rise Lin
articles.x: JERRABOMBERRA, Australia — November 10, 2026 — lululemon is launching a limited capsule in Australia and New Zealand featuring two core run styles made with enzymatically recycled polyester. Developed through its long-term work with Australian-based Samsara Eco, the capsule’s Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short 2.5″ and Pace Breaker Linerless Short 7″ build on earlier product milestones by bringing enzymatically recycled polyester into high-performance products lululemon guests know and love. Material progress through circular innovation At lululemon, material progress means improving how products perform at every stage of their life, including advancing new pathways to recycle materials into new products. Samsara Eco’s technology uses enzymes to break down plastic and textile waste into molecular building blocks that can be used to make new polyester. In both shorts, enzymatically recycled polyester makes up at least 50% of the product by weight and is used in the body material. The capsule builds on lululemon’s first enzymatically recycled polyester product, the limited-edition Packable Anorak introduced in 2024, as well as earlier work with Samsara Eco on enzymatically recycled nylon 6,6. “Material progress is part of how we define performance. Advancing circular innovation takes long-term collaboration, testing, and learning across the value chain,” said Yogendra Dandapure, Chief Materials Scientist at lululemon. “Bringing enzymatically recycled polyester into two of our core run styles is another opportunity to learn how new recycling pathways that can use textile waste as an input can be integrated into our products while maintaining the performance and quality our guests expect.” Focused launches like this help lululemon and Samsara Eco better understand how new mate

articles.o: Arvind partners with unspun to bring 3D weaving technology to industrial apparel manufacturing
articles.s: Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, has partnered with US-based technology company unspun to introduce its proprietary OneWeave™ 3D weaving technology into industrial apparel manufacturing. The first two… The post Arvind partners with unspun to bring 3D weaving te
articles.x: Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, has partnered with US-based technology company unspun to introduce its proprietary OneWeave 3D weaving technology into industrial apparel manufacturing. The first two machines are being installed at Arvind’s facility in Ahmedabad, marking the transition of the technology from unspun’s microfactory in Emeryville, California, to the production floor of a global Tier-1 manufacturer. As unspun’s first machine customer, Arvind is working with the company to establish a pathway for deploying more than 30 additional machines across India and/or North America during 2027–28, with further expansion aligned to demand from global apparel brands. Karan Ojha, CEO – Wovens Business & COE, Arvind Limited Arne Arens, Chair of the Board, unspun The partnership brings together Arvind’s extensive textile manufacturing expertise and unspun’s advanced 3D weaving technology, with a shared ambition to make apparel production more responsive, automated and resource-efficient. Under the arrangement, Arvind is purchasing the machines, while unspun will provide installation, commissioning, training, software, and ongoing service and technical support. Global apparel brands will work directly with Arvind to develop and manufacture garments using the technology. Transforming the Journey from Yarn to Garment OneWeave represents a significant departure from conventional apparel manufacturing. The technology weaves yarn directly into three-dimensional garment forms, bypassing the need for conventional two-dimensional fabric production, most cutting operations and much of the sewing process. According to unspun, a pant leg can be woven in approximately 10 minutes, with each machine capable of producing around 27,000 pants annually.

articles.x: S. Sundaravadivel, President – Operations, Pallavaa Group, has spent four decades in the textile industry, including 27 years with Pallavaa, building his career around technology, manufacturing and the discipline of the shop floor. But beyond machines and manufacturing, there is a more personal side to his journey — a love for trekking and the mountains, a fascination with weather and monsoon patterns, and a deep interest in farming and agricultural value addition. His journey offers a glimpse of a professional whose curiosity extends well beyond textiles, shaped by discipline, continuous learning and a desire to explore new horizons. For most textile professionals who have known S. Sundaravadivel over the years, he is likely to be remembered first as the technology-driven operations professional at the heart of Pallavaa Group’s manufacturing journey. His career has been shaped by machines, shop floors, maintenance, spinning technology, productivity, quality and the relentless pursuit of manufacturing consistency. S. Sundaravadivel, President – Operations, Pallavaa Group But there is another Sundaravadivel. Away from the factory, he has an unusual fascination with weather and climate patterns, follows ocean temperatures and monsoon movements, maintains a farm with around 700–750 coconut trees, takes a keen interest in value addition in agriculture and places considerable emphasis on fitness and disciplined living. After four decades in textiles, he has developed an approach to life that is remarkably similar to his approach to manufacturing: observe carefully, understand the variables, maintain discipline and keep improving. articles.o: Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster launched in Bangladesh
articles.s: A three-year Dutch-Bangladeshi initiative will connect regenerative cotton farming, garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling to advance circularity across Bangladesh’s textile value chain. Bangladesh’s transition towards a circular textile industry has gained momentum with the launch of t
articles.x: A three-year Dutch-Bangladeshi initiative will connect regenerative cotton farming, garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling to advance circularity across Bangladesh’s textile value chain. Bangladesh’s transition towards a circular textile industry has gained momentum with the launch of the Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, a three-year initiative connecting regenerative cotton cultivation with garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling. Figure 1: The Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, formally launched in Dhaka Formally launched in Dhaka on 4 November 2026, the initiative brings together international brands, textile manufacturers, recycling specialists, technology providers and research institutions from Bangladesh and the Netherlands. Its primary objective is to demonstrate how cotton can pass through successive production and recycling cycles while retaining its quality and commercial value, targeting two complete recycling cycles by 2029. Led by Raddis Cotton, the consortium includes Dutch partners Zeeman, Company Fits, Avans University of Applied Sciences and Common Era, alongside Bangladesh-based Reverse Resources. Advance Consulting and Clean & Unique are supporting the project as subcontractors. The initiative is funded by the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO). The project addresses key challenges facing Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry, including dependence on imported virgin cotton, inefficient textile waste recovery, and increasing international requirements for sustainability and supply chain traceability. articles.x: Registration has opened for the winter edition of Functional Fabric Fair powered by Performance Days, which will take place from 27-29 January 2027 at the Orange County Convention Center in Orlando, Florida. The event will run alongside the PGA Show, the golf industry’s largest annual business gathering, bringing performance textile suppliers into closer contact with apparel brands, designers and product developers working across golf, racquet sports, outdoor and activewear markets. Expanded from two days to three, Functional Fabric Fair Winter will occupy the Tangerine Ballroom at the convention centre, adjacent to the PGA Show’s West Halls E and F. Both events will operate on the same dates and opening hours, although separate registration is required. More than 100 carefully selected exhibitors are expected to present high-performance fabrics, functional materials and textile technologies, with a particular emphasis on sustainability, durability and responsible sourcing. The exhibition will also feature its established Expert Talks programme and Trend Forum, providing insights into emerging material developments, performance requirements and sustainability trends influencing the sportswear and activewear sectors. “Golf apparel is one of the most active categories for performance fabric innovation, and brands want suppliers who deliver on function, durability and sustainability,” said Steve McCullough, Event Vice President, Functional Fabric Fair. “Placing the fair alongside the PGA Show puts those suppliers in the same building as the designers and product developers who need them, during a week when the whole golf industry is in Orlando.” The co-location reflects growing opportunities for textile manufacturers and suppliers as golf apparel increasingly draws on tech

articles.o: Innovation must become a culture, not an occasional activity
articles.s: When Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry began its journey several decades ago, the gap in productivity and efficiency was much wider, while profit margins were relatively comfortable. At that s...
articles.x: When Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry began its journey several decades ago, the gap in productivity and efficiency was much wider, while profit margins were relatively comfortable. At that stage, factories could still grow without giving enough attention to continuous innovation. Figure: Engr. ATM Mahbubul Alam Milton, Executive Director, Masco Group & Member of the Steering Board, Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE). Today, the situation is very different. Margins are tighter, energy costs are increasing, competition is stronger and buyers are becoming more demanding. If we genuinely want to sustain this industry and remain competitive, there is no alternative to innovation. One of the problems is that we often make innovation sound much more difficult than it really is. We tend to confuse innovation with invention. Invention may require extensive research, technical knowledge, funding, time and patience. Innovation, however, can begin with a much simpler mindset: identifying a problem and finding a better way to solve it. Innovation does not always have to mean a breakthrough technology or a completely new product. A small process modification, better utility management, improved operating practice, smarter use of data or stronger coordination between departments can all be forms of innovation. These changes may appear small individually, but when they are practiced consistently across an organization, their combined impact can be significant. We can see this clearly in utilities, dyeing and production management. At Masco Group, for example, we have analysed our utility requirements and improvement opportunities up to 2030. articles.o: Overcoming the polypropylene dyeing barrier
articles.s: Japan’s Prime Polymer and US biomaterials specialist Newlight Technologies have developed a new textile material that combines the lightweight properties of polypropylene (PP) with dyeability comparable to polyester. The development could significantly expand the use of PP in apparel and footwear, w
articles.x: Japan’s Prime Polymer and US biomaterials specialist Newlight Technologies have developed a new textile material that combines the lightweight properties of polypropylene (PP) with dyeability comparable to polyester. The development could significantly expand the use of PP in apparel and footwear, where its low density, durability and moisture management properties have long been attractive, but its resistance to conventional dyeing processes has restricted its adoption. PP is one of the lightest commercially available textile polymers, with a density of approximately 0.91 g/cm³ compared to around 1.38 g/cm³ for polyester. It also absorbs very little moisture, making it particularly suitable for next-to-skin garments, sportswear and applications where rapid drying is important. Its highly crystalline, non-polar molecular structure, however, makes it extremely difficult to dye using conventional textile processes. As a result, PP fibres are generally coloured by adding pigments to the polymer melt before extrusion, limiting flexibility in colour selection and subsequent fabric processing. The newly developed material combines Prime Polymer’s PP alloy design and compounding expertise with Newlight’s Aircarbon polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), a biologically produced polymer manufactured using microorganisms that convert methane into useful materials. The resulting polymer alloy can be processed from compound pellets into yarns and subsequently converted into knitted or woven fabrics. Crucially, the companies report that the resulting textiles can be dyed using conventional disperse dye systems, achieving colouration comparable to that of polyester. articles.o: Landmark Partnership Between Unspun And Arvind Limited
articles.s: AHMEDABAD, India & SAN FRANCISCO — November 9, 2026 — unspun, the B Corp-certified fashion technology company behind OneWeave™ 3D weaving, and Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, today announced a strategic partnership to bring yarn-to-garment 3D weaving into indu
articles.x: AHMEDABAD, India & SAN FRANCISCO — November 9, 2026 — unspun, the B Corp-certified fashion technology company behind OneWeave 3D weaving, and Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, today announced a strategic partnership to bring yarn-to-garment 3D weaving into industrial-scale apparel manufacturing. The deployment marks Arvind’s first installation of OneWeave technology and the first time unspun’s 3D weaving platform will move from its own microfactory into the production environment of a global Tier-1 manufacturer — an important step in the company’s broader vision for more responsive, automated and lower-waste apparel supply chains. The fashion industry’s operating model still depends heavily on forecasting demand months in advance, committing to bulk orders, and correcting for inevitable misses through markdowns, deadstock and disposal. McKinsey has reported that U.S. retailers alone were sitting on approximately $740 billion in unsold goods in 2023. As of July 19, 2026, new EU rules prohibit large companies from destroying unsold clothes, clothing accessories and footwear across the EU — a policy shift that makes overproduction not just a sustainability problem, but a compliance and business-model risk. In apparel manufacturing, conventional cut-and-sew production also creates fabric offcuts before a garment ever reaches a customer — making waste, excess inventory and long lead times structural problems rather than edge cases. Under the partnership, Arvind will deploy two OneWeave machines at its facility in Ahmedabad, India, with operations expected to begin by December 2026. The phased partnership includes a path to 30+ additional machines across India and/or North America in 2027–28, scaling with demand from global apparel brands

articles.o: Lectra PLM cuts time for Missoni
articles.s: Italian fashion and home textiles brand Missoni has reduced the time spent managing and maintaining product data by an estimated 60% following the implementation of Lectra’s Kubix Link product lifecycle management (PLM) system. The cloud-based platform has been introduced as part of Missoni’s decisi
articles.x: Italian fashion and home textiles brand Missoni has reduced the time spent managing and maintaining product data by an estimated 60% following the implementation of Lectra’s Kubix Link product lifecycle management (PLM) system. The cloud-based platform has been introduced as part of Missoni’s decision to bring the management of its Missoni Home business in-house, requiring new operational processes and closer integration between product development, production, quality control and supply chain partners. Founded in 1953 by Ottavio and Rosita Missoni, the Milan-based company is internationally recognised for its distinctive knitwear, colours and geometric patterns. Its activities have expanded beyond fashion into home textiles, furnishings and accessories. Missoni has worked with Lectra for more than 25 years, initially introducing the company’s CAD solutions in the early 2000s. The latest project involved implementing Kubix Link to centralise product information and establish a common platform for managing collections and coordinating activities across departments. Following an initial analysis phase, the system went live after a 12-month implementation period and has since been adopted by more than 40 users across product development, merchandising, quality control and compliance. More than 20 suppliers and subcontractors have also been given direct access to technical product information, reducing the need for email exchanges and improving coordination throughout the supply chain. Missoni now manages more than 20,000 stock keeping units (SKUs) through the system and creates almost 1,000 new items annually. articles.s: Groz-Beckert, the German manufacturer of industrial needles, precision components and textile machinery accessories, will introduce new developments across all of its six principal product areas, at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026, taking place in Shanghai from November 20-24th. articles.x: Groz-Beckert, the German manufacturer of industrial needles, precision components and textile machinery accessories, will introduce new developments across all of its six principal product areas, at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026, taking place in Shanghai from November 20-24th. A specific emphasis will be on reducing energy consumption, extending component service life and improving processing performance. Among the highlights is a new energy-saving, maintenance-free cylinder wire for spinning applications, designed to increase card output while reducing maintenance requirements and extending operating life. Further developments in stationary flats and revolving tops can improve carding performance, including new configurations for processing fine yarns and adapting to the latest generation of carding machines. In circular knitting, Groz-Beckert will highlight its LCmax needle technology, which employs a wave-shaped shank geometry to reduce friction and energy consumption during operation. The company is also addressing the growing complexity of technical and medical textiles with its San TT flat knitting needle, developed specifically for producing particularly tight stitch structures. Another development, the San FY, is designed to improve processing reliability and fabric appearance when working with irregular effect yarns. Fine-gauge knitting technology will be demonstrated in collaboration with Chinese flat knitting machine specialist Sinotex, with a knitted collar illustrating the potential for producing finer fabrics and tighter stitch structures. Glass yarn demands Technical textiles are also a focus of the company’s weaving developments, particularly in the production of fabrics used in printed circuit boards and other electronic applications. articles.x: Texworld Apparel Sourcing Paris will celebrate its 30th anniversary from 25-27 January 2027 at the Paris-Le-Bourget Exhibition Centre, bringing together international fabric manufacturers, garment producers and sourcing professionals. Organised by Messe Frankfurt France, the anniversary edition will introduce a redesigned layout across Halls 3 and 4, aimed at strengthening connections between fabrics and finished products while improving visitor navigation. The new configuration will accommodate the event’s two principal areas: Texworld, dedicated to fabrics and raw materials, and Apparel Sourcing, which focuses on finished garments and accessories. Networking spaces, trend forums, conference areas and visitor services will be distributed across both halls to encourage interaction between exhibitors and buyers. More than 1,000 international exhibitors are expected, offering a broad selection of textile materials and finished products. Strong participation is anticipated from Indian manufacturers, reflecting growing interest in the European market and the potential opportunities arising from the proposed EU-India free trade agreement. The agreement, currently undergoing ratification and expected to enter into force in 2027, could eliminate European import duties on Indian textiles and garments, which currently reach up to 12% depending on the product. Trend forums dedicated to Spring/Summer 2028 collections will feature in both exhibition halls. articles.o: INDA Announces New Name For International Fiber Journal
articles.s: CARY, N.C. — November 9, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, and its publishing arm INDA Media are excited to announce that International Fiber Journal (IFJ) will become Fibers&Nonwovens with Issue 1, 2027. The new name reflects the magazine’s longstanding focus on fiber i
articles.x: CARY, N.C. — November 9, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, and its publishing arm INDA Media are excited to announce that International Fiber Journal (IFJ) will become Fibers&Nonwovens with Issue 1, 2027. The new name reflects the magazine’s longstanding focus on fiber innovation and its coverage of the materials, technologies and markets shaping the global nonwovens industry. Under its new name, the magazine will continue to deliver the industry reporting, market insights and technical perspectives that IFJ readers rely on. “Fibers, materials science, nonwovens and engineered materials have long been part of the same story for our readers,” said Rachael Davis, publisher and chief content officer, INDA Media. “An advance in fiber technology can change how a nonwoven is made, how it performs and where it can be used. Our job is to follow those connections and help readers understand what new developments mean for their work. The name Fibers&Nonwovens makes that editorial focus clear while carrying forward the technical reporting and industry perspectives readers have come to expect from International Fiber Journal.” INDA acquired International Fiber Journal and International Filtration News in October 2018. At the time, IFJ covered man-made fibers, technical textiles and nonwovens, connecting producers of engineered materials and machinery with fiber and yarn users in more than 90 countries. Current subscribers will continue to receive the new magazine without interruption. For subscription information, please email circulation@inda.org. The 2027 Media Kit is now available. This season, the collection places a strong emphasis on layering and versatile styling, exploring how different textures, silhouettes and winter essentials can be combined to create complete looks for changing temperatures and occasions. Rich textures, warm layers and clean silhouettes shape the collection, while thoughtful details give each piece a polished yet wearable character. The pieces have been designed to work both individually and as part of layered outfits, allowing different combinations to be created throughout the season. From lighter everyday layering to more structured winter looks, Winter Edit 2026 offers styling options suited to workdays, casual outings, gatherings and seasonal occasions. The focus on mix-and-match dressing also allows individual pieces to be styled in different ways, giving customers more flexibility in building their winter wardrobes. According to Blucheez, the collection was developed with the idea that winter dressing should feel comfortable and practical while still allowing room for personal style. The balance of texture, proportion and layering brings a contemporary character to the range without making the looks feel overly complicated. articles.x: Three-year Dutch-Bangladeshi partnership will connect regenerative cotton farming, garment waste recovery and fibre-to-fibre recycling, with a target to demonstrate two complete recycling cycles by 2029 A new Dutch-Bangladeshi initiative is seeking to change how Bangladesh produces, recovers and reuses cotton by connecting regenerative agriculture with garment waste recycling and traceable textile manufacturing. Figure 1: The Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, formally launched in Dhaka. The Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, formally launched in Dhaka on 4 November 2026, will test whether cotton can move through successive production and recycling cycles while retaining commercial value. The three-year project brings together textile producers, international brands, recycling specialists, technology providers and researchers to develop a model that could eventually be adopted across Bangladesh's textile and apparel industry. Figure 2: Janna van der Linden, Deputy Head of Mission at the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Led by Raddis Cotton, the consortium includes Dutch partners Zeeman, Company Fits, Avans University of Applied Sciences and Common Era, alongside Bangladesh-based Reverse Resources. Advance Consulting and Clean & Unique are supporting the initiative as subcontractors. In addition, this project was funded by RVO. The project comes as Bangladesh faces growing pressure to reduce its dependence on imported cotton, recover more value from textile waste and prepare for increasingly demanding sustainability and traceability requirements in international markets. articles.o: CHT Group advances PP-free denim finishing through industry collaboration
articles.s: The global denim industry is facing growing pressure to reduce its use of potassium permanganate (PP), a chemical widely used to create faded and vintage effects in denim garments. In response, CHT Gr...
articles.x: The global denim industry is facing growing pressure to reduce its use of potassium permanganate (PP), a chemical widely used to create faded and vintage effects in denim garments. In response, CHT Group is providing technical support to the PP-free Denim Mission, an industry initiative developed by Ruess Group to accelerate the adoption of scalable alternatives to conventional PP-based finishing processes. Caption The mission aims to promote production methods that can deliver consistent denim fading effects without relying on potassium permanganate. With CHT Group's technical expertise, the initiative seeks to support the industry's transition towards safer chemical management and commercially viable finishing technologies. The scale of the challenge is significant. An industry report estimates that nearly 2,000 tons of potassium permanganate are used in denim finishing each year globally. Separately, CHT estimates that global production consumes around 250,000 liters of permanganate solution daily. PP use raises concerns over worker exposure, chemical handling, and wastewater management. Its inclusion in the Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals (ZDHC) Chemical Watchlist in 2026 is also increasing industry attention on alternatives. Several technologies are being explored, including enzyme-based bleaching, laser and ozone finishing. However, replacing PP requires more than introducing another chemical. Alternative processes must deliver consistent fading effects, maintain garment quality, and remain commercially viable at industrial scale. A separate denim finishing study by Environmental Impact Measuring (EIM) and BCome demonstrated the potential of alternative technologies. Another textile complex under the Kurt Baver brand is planned in Bukhara city, with an annual production capacity of 62,000 tons. The two textile developments are expected to increase the share of higher-value-added products to 65% and generate an additional $100 million in export revenue. Energy investment is another major part of the regional development plan. Bukhara has attracted around $2 billion in renewable energy investment in recent years. The region has commissioned 1,000 MW of wind power and 750 MW of solar power, alongside 63 MW of energy storage capacity. Further projects are expected to expand generation capacity. ACWA Power is developing a 300 MW wind power plant in Gijduvan district. Toyota Corporation and China’s Sinoma are also constructing wind power facilities with a combined capacity of 1,000 MW in Jondor and Peshku districts. The region is also planning a $165 million waste-to-energy project with Chinese partners. The project will generate electricity from municipal waste in Kagan district. The combined investment strategy highlights the growing link between textile industrialization and energy infrastructure. articles.x: A well-made pair of loafers can bring the entire look together. With the launch of its Signature Suede Loafers , Blucheez introduces a refined footwear option designed for modern everyday dressing. Crafted from high-quality suede, the loafers feature a soft texture, clean silhouette and carefully finished details. The design feels polished without looking overly formal, making it easy to wear across different occasions. The Blucheez Signature Suede Loafers are designed to move easily between different styles and settings. They can be paired with tailored trousers and formal outfits for a sharper appearance, styled with relaxed separates for a smart casual look, or worn with more elevated evening and party outfits. This versatility makes the loafers suitable for formal wear, casual dressing, party wear and refined everyday use. Rather than following short-term trends, Blucheez has focused on a timeless design that feels modern, comfortable and easy to style. The suede finish adds depth and character, while the streamlined shape keeps the overall look elegant and understated. The launch also marks a new chapter in Blucheez’s approach to complete dressing, where footwear plays an important role in defining the final look. With its balance of quality, simplicity and contemporary styling, the Signature Suede Loafers are designed to become an easy addition to a well-considered wardrobe. Blucheez Signature Suede Loafers are now available both online and at Blucheez outlets. articles.x: EVANSTON, Ill. — November 4, 2026 — NylaNova, a chemical recycling company built on technology from Northwestern University, today announced a partnership with Nylene under which NylaNova will supply Nylene with green caprolactam recovered from post-consumer nylon-6 waste. Caprolactam is the raw material used to make nylon, and Nylene is an established nylon-6 producer with operations in the United States and Canada. Nylene has been producing specialty nylon resins, copolymers, and compounds for decades, supplying the automotive, packaging, wire and cable, injection molding, roto molding, fiber, and carpet industries. The company is also long established in nylon recycling, operating a nylon-6 depolymerization process at its Arnprior, Ontario facility, one of only three such units in the world and the longest continuously running. Under the partnership, NylaNova’s green caprolactam becomes an additional supply source for their nylon-6 production. It is an important step as NylaNova builds a broader network of partners to bring recycled nylon-6 back into production. Yosi Kratish, Founder and CTO of NylaNova Nylon-6 is used across apparel, carpet, and industrial applications, and roughly 2.75 million tonnes of it are discarded worldwide each year. Almost none of that material is turned back into nylon, making it one of the most difficult plastics to return to the supply chain. At the same time, recycled-content requirements are tightening. Mandates are now law in California and New York, textile and carpet EPR bills are advancing in six more states, and EU textile EPR schemes must be in place by April 2028. articles.o: Why stretch denim remains a recycling challenge
articles.s: A pair of stretch jeans offers comfort, flexibility, and a better fit. A small amount of elastane helps denim stretch and recover its shape after wear. However, this performance comes with an end-of-l...
articles.x: A pair of stretch jeans offers comfort, flexibility, and a better fit. A small amount of elastane helps denim stretch and recover its shape after wear. However, this performance comes with an end-of-life challenge. When blended with cotton, elastane can complicate textile recycling and limit the recovery of usable fibers. The challenge for denim manufacturers is to preserve comfort while designing garments for a more circular future. Figure: Italian denim manufacturer Candiani Denim developed COREVA technology using natural rubber yarn instead of synthetic stretch yarn. Courtesy: Collected Elastane, also known as spandex, is difficult to separate from other fibers using many existing recycling technologies. Mechanical recycling shreds fabric into fibers, which can become shorter and weaker. Even low elastane content can disrupt textile-to-textile recycling, according to Fashion for Good. Its Stretching Circularity project, launched in February 2026, is evaluating bio-based and recycled elastane alternatives alongside technologies for separating and recovering blended fibers. The project aims to generate comparable data on performance, environmental impact, commercial feasibility, and scalability. Reconsidering fabric construction The first step is to reconsider where stretch is necessary. Mechanical stretch uses yarn structure, twist, and fabric construction to provide flexibility without a separate elastic fiber. Low-elastane designs offer another option for products that need limited stretch and recovery. However, manufacturers must test durability, fit retention, fabric growth, and recovery after repeated wear and washing before adopting these approaches commercially. articles.x: DURHAM, N.C. — November 6, 2026 — The American Association of Textile Chemists and Colorists (AATCC) is strengthening its visibility across the global textile marketplace, with its upcoming exhibition at ITMA ASIA + CITME in Shanghai, November 20–24, a major focus of that effort. Following Functional Fabric Fair Fall in Portland and alongside its participation in this week’s Advanced Textiles Expo in Orlando, AATCC is bringing its expertise directly to the places where textile professionals connect, discover technologies, and make business decisions. Connecting in Shanghai AATCC’s presence in Shanghai underscores its commitment to building relationships across China, Asia, and the broader international textile community. Taking place at the National Exhibition and Convention Center, ITMA ASIA + CITME brings together technologies spanning textile production, processing, recycling, and testing. For AATCC, the exhibition provides an important opportunity to reach new audiences, engage existing members and partners, and broaden awareness of its standards, educational programs, and technical resources. At Hall 6.1, Stand A25, visitors can connect directly with AATCC representatives and explore interactive displays and tools supporting textile quality and performance evaluation. Featured resources include color evaluation scales, lightfastness testing materials, and details on evaluating water resistance and repellency. AATCC representatives will discuss how standardized testing supports consistent results and how professionals can connect with the association through education, membership, and technical collaboration. articles.x: Reju is working with six textile mills in Europe and the Americas to develop finished fabrics from regenerated polyester, as it prepares to establish an international network of industrial-scale textile recycling facilities. The Paris-based company, owned by Technip Energies, is collaborating with A. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics, Utenos Trikotažas and Swisstex Direct to demonstrate how polyester recovered from post-consumer textile waste can be incorporated into commercially viable fabrics. The partnerships represent an important step in connecting Reju’s planned recycling operations with downstream textile manufacturing, helping to establish a supply chain for regenerated polyester. Reju is developing a chemical recycling process based on technology originating from IBM Research, designed to recover polyester from discarded textiles and return it to the textile supply chain without the quality limitations associated with conventional mechanical recycling. The company is progressing plans for a network of Regeneration Hubs capable of processing post-consumer polyester waste at industrial scale. Alongside establishing recycling capacity, Reju is seeking to demonstrate that its regenerated materials can be processed efficiently by existing textile manufacturers while meeting the quality and performance requirements of apparel brands. The six participating mills bring complementary manufacturing capabilities covering knitted and woven fabrics, dyeing, finishing and garment production. In Portugal, A. Sampaio contributes more than 75 years of experience in circular knitted fabrics, while RDD Textiles specialises in advanced knitted constructions, recycled and bio-based materials and innovative dyeing technologies. articles.o: Nuyarn wins Performance Days Wool Award
articles.s: Nuyarn Technologies has received the 2026 Performance Days Wool Award for an innovative open-net fabric construction developed in collaboration with Takisada Corporation, highlighting the potential of advanced wool technologies for high-performance apparel. The award recognises a lightweight fabric
articles.x: Nuyarn Technologies has received the 2026 Performance Days Wool Award for an innovative open-net fabric construction developed in collaboration with Takisada Corporation, highlighting the potential of advanced wool technologies for high-performance apparel. The award recognises a lightweight fabric structure designed to maximise breathability and manage moisture at the vapour stage, supporting improved comfort during demanding physical activity. The development combines Nuyarn’s proprietary yarn technology with specialist fabric engineering to extend the performance capabilities of natural fibres. “This award reflects our ongoing drive to push the boundaries of performance textiles. Alongside our partners at Takisada Corporation, it demonstrates what’s possible when continuous innovation, fabric development, and strong partnerships come together,” said Andy Wynne, CEO of Nuyarn. The open-net construction offers potential applications across a broad range of performance apparel, from ultralight summer endurance garments to technical base layers for high-intensity alpine activities. Its structure is designed to facilitate moisture vapour transfer while retaining the durability, elasticity and thermoregulation required in modern activewear. At the heart of the development is Nuyarn’s twist-free spinning technology, which differs from conventional wool processing methods that tightly twist fibres together. By reducing the constraints imposed by traditional spinning, the technology is designed to preserve more of wool’s natural performance characteristics. articles.x: By MK Prabhakar For Sulochana Cotton Mills, sustainability has been more than a response to an industry-wide trend. Over the years, the Tirupur-based textile major has built a strong reputation for developing and adopting innovative solutions aimed at reducing waste and promoting circularity across the textile value chain. Its pioneering initiatives in PET bottle recycling and post-industrial waste recycling have been among the key highlights of this journey. Sabhari Girish, Head of Sustainability, Sulochana Cotton Mills With sustainability continuing to remain an important part of its growth strategy, Sulochana is now looking at taking its efforts a step further. The company is planning to expand its manufacturing footprint beyond its existing six units, while simultaneously investing in textile-to-textile recycling, smart manufacturing and garmenting. We caught up with Sabhari Girish, Head of Sustainability, Sulochana Cotton Mills, for an exclusive interaction to understand the company’s performance during FY 2025-26 and its plans for the coming years. Navigating a Challenging FY 2025-26 Reflecting on the group’s performance during FY 2025-26, Girish said the year presented its share of challenges, particularly due to tariff-related uncertainties. “Just as in the case with others in the textile industry, the sailing was not so smooth for us. The tariff turbulence came as a dampener. When it comes to fabric, we have a lot of exposure to the US market, so that played a spoilsport,” he said. However, the company’s strong market relationships and continued focus on innovation helped it navigate the challenging environment. “The trust that we have built in the market and our innovation focus helped us navigate the choppy waters without any major trouble. The concept gives a name to technical membr
articles.x: PORT ST. LUCIE, Fla. — November 5, 2026 — Serge Ferrari North America, the North American subsidiary of Serge Ferrari Group, which designs, develops, and manufactures innovative composite materials, introduces the 7th Material to the North American market. The concept gives a name to technical membranes—lightweight, flexible composite fabrics used across architecture for roofing, facades, shading, and interior applications. Beijing Taikang Yanyuan Health&Wellness Center Serge Ferrari Group unveiled the 7th Material at its global launch event on Sept. 24, 2026, establishing it as an open industry category rather than a product line or trademark. The concept positions technical membranes as a seventh construction material category, alongside stone, earth, wood, concrete, metal, and glass. “We are not launching a new product; we are giving a name to a material family that is already present in architecture but still insufficiently recognized,” said Sébastien Baril, CEO of Serge Ferrari Group. “With the 7th Material, we want to show that performance can also come from the behavior of a surface, its lightness, and its ability to combine multiple functions. This category is intended to be open, documented, and shared across the whole industry.” For nearly 50 years, technical membranes have been used in architecture, yet they are often grouped broadly with “lightweight” materials and specified only after a building has already been designed. The 7th Material concept aims to bring membranes into the design process earlier. While the six historic materials are classified by their composition, the 7th Material is defined by its function, deriving performance from a surface under tension rather than from mass and added layers. articles.x: Detlef Fischer is the owner and CEO of TEXTILCOLOR AG, a Swiss specialty chemicals company based in Sevelen, Switzerland. Under his leadership, TEXTILCOLOR combines extensive expertise in textile chemistry with practical application technology and customer-specific solutions. The company supports its customers throughout the textile value chain — from pretreatment and dyeing to printing and the functional finishing and coating of textiles. TEXTILCOLOR stands for sustainable, environmentally friendly solutions, modern infrastructure and a clear focus on the future of sustainable textile production. Our objective is to develop solutions that deliver consistent technical performance while helping textile manufacturers reduce their environmental impact and use resources more efficiently. A key element is the development of highly effective dyes and textile auxiliaries that support more efficient dyeing and finishing processes. articles.s: The 2026 anniversary edition connected circular materials, performance fabrics and AI with international sourcing, showing how Taiwan’s textile expertise can serve the next generation of products. By Nithin Kumar TITAS… The post TITAS at 30: Taiwan Turns Textile Innovation into Global Opportunity ap
articles.x: The 2026 anniversary edition connected circular materials, performance fabrics and AI with international sourcing, showing how Taiwan’s textile expertise can serve the next generation of products. By Nithin Kumar TITAS 2026 made the connections between material development, garment design and factory performance easier to see. Its 30th edition paired recovered fibres and functional fabrics with finished concept garments and digital production tools, giving buyers concrete examples of how Taiwan’s textile capabilities can support their next product. Held from 6 to 8 October at Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, Hall 1, the 30th Taipei Innovative Textile Application Show brought together 410 exhibitors from 12 countries across 977 booths. Organiser Taiwan Textile Federation (TTF) reported approximately 30,405 buyer visits over the three days and estimated future business opportunities at US$60 million. Since its debut in 1997, TITAS has given Taiwanese suppliers a shared platform for reaching international brands. Its 30th edition put that role into perspective: functional fabric development is increasingly connected with circular design and digital production, broadening the scope of the sourcing conversation. The sourcing programme connected more than 70 international brands from 16 markets with Taiwanese exhibitors in over 900 procurement meetings. Visiting delegations also came from India, Japan, South Korea, Vietnam and Thailand. The new Italian pavilion, organised by the Italian Trade Agency with ACIMIT, brought 11 machinery companies, including FADIS, Color Service, Corino and Danitech. articles.t: 혁신은 Bangladesh 섬유 산업의 다음 장을 정의할 것입니다
articles.o: Innovation will define next chapter of Bangladesh’s textile industry
articles.s: Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry is entering a period where cost competitiveness alone will no longer be enough to secure future growth. Rising production costs, changing buyer expectations...
articles.x: Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry is entering a period where cost competitiveness alone will no longer be enough to secure future growth. Rising production costs, changing buyer expectations, rapid technological advancement and the growing demand for higher-value and sustainable products are pushing the industry to build stronger capabilities in knowledge, research and innovation. Figure: Prof. Dr. Engr. Ayub Nabi Khan,Vice Chancellor, BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT) & Member of the Steering Board, Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE). For Prof. Dr. Engr. Ayub Nabi Khan , Vice Chancellor of BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT), this transition will depend heavily on how effectively Bangladesh connects industry with academia. He believes universities must move closer to factory realities, strengthen research in advanced materials and technologies, and prepare engineers for AI, automation, digital manufacturing, sustainability and product diversification. Speaking to Textile Today , Prof. Khan discusses the skills Bangladesh needs to compete on value, the gap between textile education and modern manufacturing, the commercialization of academic research, opportunities in MMF and technical textiles, and the need for deeper industry-academia collaboration. He also highlights the role of platforms such as Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) and the upcoming TIE–ITET Textile Innovation Expo 2026 in bringing researchers, factories, engineers, technology providers and young innovators closer together. articles.o: Reju targets industrial-scale production of recycled knitted fabrics
articles.s: Recycled polyester specialist Reju has partnered with a group of circular knitting mills to expand the industrial-scale production of post-consumer textile-to-textile recycled fabrics. Figure: Access...
articles.x: Recycled polyester specialist Reju has partnered with a group of circular knitting mills to expand the industrial-scale production of post-consumer textile-to-textile recycled fabrics. Figure: Access to high-volume jersey production and certified dyeing and finishing processes will support the development of recycled fabrics for wider textile applications. The partnerships will give Reju access to different circular knitting and fabric manufacturing processes. These include circular knit design, chain-of-custody verified recycling, high-volume jersey production, and sustainability-certified dyeing and finishing. The collaboration aims to connect recycled polyester production with the capabilities needed to manufacture finished fabrics at commercial scale. It will help Reju move regenerated polyester from recycled raw materials to market-ready knitted fabrics. Access to high-volume jersey production and certified dyeing and finishing processes will support the development of recycled fabrics for wider textile applications. The partnerships also highlight the importance of cooperation between recycling companies and textile mills in building a textile-to-textile recycling supply chain. Scaling recycled polyester into finished fabrics requires not only recycling technology but also access to established knitting, dyeing, and finishing facilities. Reju's approach focuses on expanding the use of post-consumer textile waste as a feedstock for new polyester fabrics.

articles.s: At ITMA ASIA 2026, KARL MAYER will demonstrate its expertise in processing staple fibers during warp preparation and will return to where this technology belongs: the Weaving Hall, at Booth 3/A24. The focus here will be on the latest-generation WARPDIRECT direct warping machine, featuring various ya
articles.x: At ITMA ASIA 2026, KARL MAYER will demonstrate its expertise in processing staple fibers during warp preparation and will return to where this technology belongs: the Weaving Hall, at Booth 3/A24 . The focus here will be on the latest-generation WARPDIRECT direct warping machine, featuring various yarn tensioners, as well as the sophisticated HSB Size Box – the centerpiece of the innovative PROSIZE sizing machine. Both technologies are aimed specifically at manufacturers of high-quality goods in the commodity sector. „Our machines produce warp beams of the highest quality with high process efficiency. This offers particular advantages to textile manufacturers who are focused on generating real added value in a highly competitive market,“ says Enzo Paoli, President of the Warp Preparation Business Unit at KARL MAYER. WARPDIRECT: With the highest speed to precision warp beams Since its launch at the end of last year, the WARPDIRECT 2.0 has already been successfully deployed worldwide. Its performance is particularly valued in India, but also in China and Europe. Its strengths include identical warping lengths for all warp beams and high production output. In practice, warping speeds of up to 1,200 m/min are achieved. In addition, the current machine version stands out thanks to an upgrade to the press roll system. The change from hydraulic to electric operation reduces maintenance requirements while ensuring precise warping quality. In combination with an optimal yarn depositing device, this results in completely cylindrical beams with precise yarn arrangement. articles.x: Reju is working with six textile mills in Europe and the Americas to develop finished fabrics from regenerated polyester, as it prepares to establish an international network of industrial-scale textile recycling facilities. The Paris-based company, owned by Technip Energies, is collaborating with A. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics, Utenos Trikotažas and Swisstex Direct to demonstrate how polyester recovered from post-consumer textile waste can be incorporated into commercially viable fabrics. These partnerships represent an important step in connecting Reju’s planned recycling operations with downstream textile manufacturing. Reju is developing a chemical recycling process based on technology originating from IBM Research, with the aim of recovering polyester from discarded textiles and returning it to the textile supply chain without the quality limitations associated with conventional mechanical recycling. The company is currently progressing plans for a network of Regeneration Hubs capable of processing post-consumer polyester waste at industrial scale. Establishing recycling capacity, however, is only one part of the challenge – ensuring regenerated materials can be processed efficiently by existing textile manufacturers and meet the performance requirements of brands is equally important. The six participating mills will provide a range of complementary manufacturing capabilities. In Portugal, A. Sampaio contributes more than 75 years of experience in circular knitted fabrics, while RDD Textiles specialises in other knitted constructions, recycled and bio-based materials and advanced dyeing technologies. articles.x: The ZDHC Foundation today launched Version 4.0 of its ZDHC Manufacturing Restricted Substances List (ZDHC MRSL). This update reflects the latest scientific developments and evolving industry needs. The ZDHC Manufacturing Restricted Substances List provides a harmonized, science-based framework for restricting hazardous substances in chemical formulations used during manufacturing. Unlike traditional Restricted Substances Lists, which focus on finished products, the ZDHC MRSL addresses chemicals at their source, helping to prevent hazardous substances from entering production processes in the first place. ZDHC developed the update through its established MRSL governance process and had the ZDHC MRSL Council independently assess it, drawing on scientific, regulatory, and industry evidence as well as stakeholder review. Independent governance and MRSL CouncilThe updates in ZDHC MRSL V4.0 build on the ongoing review process led by the ZDHC MRSL Council, an independent group of technical experts representing diverse segments of the textile, apparel, leather and footwear industries, alongside other relevant stakeholders. The Council uses an objective, science-based approach to assess proposed substances and recommend their inclusion in the ZDHC MRSL or MRSL Candidate List. For Version 4.0, this assessment took into account developments in relevant regulatory lists, including Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) and Substances of Very High Concern (SVHC), as well as inputs from the ZDHC Chemical Watchlist. The proposed updates also underwent a stakeholder review to gather broader industry feedback. articles.x: Dishang Group has secured the State-of-the-Art Manufacturer title at the recent 2026 Professional Clothing Industry Association Worldwide (PCIAW) Awards, retaining the accolade for the second year running. Presented at the annual sector gathering in London, it honours Dishang’s continued capital investment in industrial technology, operational agility and greener production methods across its international network. Headquartered in Weihai, Shandong Province, China, Dishang Group operates more than 90 wholly owned manufacturing sites alongside 200 production partners globally, engineering end-to-end design and garment solutions for brands with products spanning menswear, womenswear, activewear, tailoring and workwear. The consecutive win reflects rapid developments across the business since last year. Over the past twelve months, Dishang has deepened the rollout of its Smart Digital Manufacturing Initiative, embedding machine learning, robotic handling and automated data monitoring into daily factory workflows. Other highlights from the past year that helped the company retain its title include the increased use of an AI-led energy platform that now watches over 80% of Dishang’s manufacturing facilities, helping shave 12% off per-unit energy consumption compared with 2024 levels. On the factory floor, high-speed 3D digital sampling and AI-driven design tools and textile-to-textile recycling technologies continue to help reduce the environmental impact of garment production, meeting the growing retail demand for demonstrable, audited supply-chain credentials. From its UK design headquarters at The Chapel in Harrogate, Dishang (UK) acts as the direct technical and commercial channel between British and European clothing brands and the group’s far-reaching factory base. articles.x: Jury recognizes the CHT Group’s efforts to advance sustainable transformation and its integration of chemical product development with industrial customer processes CHT Germany GmbH, part of the foundation-owned CHT Group, is a finalist for the “German Sustainability Award Companies 2027” in the Large Companies size class. The CHT Group is proud that the jury has selected the company for this prestigious award. The finalist recognition honors the CHT Group’s extensive efforts to advance sustainable transformation across product development and industrial applications. The jury was particularly impressed by the integration of chemical product development with industrial customer processes. It highlights the PIGMENTURA textile dyeing process using a pad-dry process as an approach to reducing water consumption. The jury also recognizes the CHT Group’s work on product carbon footprints and its systematic assessment of critical substances. Within the CHT Group, a calculation tool supports assessing product carbon footprints as early as the product development stage. In addition, a science-based internal classification system helps identify critical substances and replace them wherever technically and economically feasible. In this way, the CHT Group incorporates key sustainability considerations from the development stage onward, connecting process design, transparency, and substance selection with the requirements of industrial applications. The company is a finalist for the German Sustainability Award Companies. articles.x: Dear Fellow Industry Owners and Colleagues, Bangladesh’s Ready-Made Garment (RMG) industry remains one of the key pillars of the national economy, contributing significantly to foreign exchange earnings, employment generation, women’s economic empowerment, and industrial development. However, ensuring the industry’s long-term sustainability requires a balanced approach that addresses fair wages, employment generation, workforce skill development, productivity enhancement, and international competitiveness. Drawing on my extensive experience in the garment industry and involvement in BGMEA’s compliance-related activities, I would like to present several observations and policy recommendations concerning Bangladesh’s existing minimum wage structure. articles.x: Karl Mayer will introduce its new Multiply BX biaxial warp knitting machine during ITMA ASIA 2026, targeting the growing demand for high-performance reinforcement textiles used in wind turbine rotor blades. The machine, developed specifically for the wind power industry, will be demonstrated at the company’s manufacturing facility in Changzhou, China, during a Product Show coinciding with the international textile machinery exhibition in Shanghai. Designed for the efficient production of biaxial non-crimp fabrics, the Multiply BX processes glass fibres into reinforcement textiles with a high proportion of filler yarns, lightweight weft yarns and long stitch lengths. These structures are particularly suited to the longitudinal reinforcement requirements of modern wind turbine blades. According to Karl Mayer, the new machine delivers productivity improvements of 20-25% compared with its established Max Glass ECO model, achieving production speeds of 1,600-2,200 min⁻¹ and output of up to 500 metres per hour, depending on stitch length. The Multiply BX achieves its highest performance at stitch lengths of 4-5 mm, commonly used in wind power applications. It accommodates filler yarns of up to 2,400 tex alongside lightweight weft yarns of 100-200 tex, which provide transverse stabilisation while maintaining the emphasis on longitudinal reinforcement. The typical weight ratio of filler to weft yarns is 6:1. Dr Jürgen Tröltzsch, Product Specialist for Composite Machines at Karl Mayer Technical Textiles. © Karl Mayer “When developing the Multiply BX, we consistently focused on the needs of our wind power customers. While most plant-based plastic alternatives are made exclusively from land crops, Uluu is one of the fi
articles.x: Norrøna, the Norwegian outdoor brand known for durable, premium outerwear, is partnering with Australian materials company Uluu to develop a new kind of performance fibre made mostly from seaweed. While most plant-based plastic alternatives are made exclusively from land crops, Uluu is one of the first to make a plastic alternative using seaweed. Together, the two companies are exploring the potential of seaweed-derived polymers as an alternative to fossil-based synthetics, advancing research into regenerative raw materials for the future of outdoor apparel. The goal is to develop fibres and fabrics tough enough for the outdoors and one day use them in Norrøna products. The work runs parallel to Norrøna’s support of Bellona’s efforts to restore Arctic kelp ecosystems impacted by sea urchin overgrazing along Norway’s northern coast. “Building the next generation of outdoor materials requires brands to get involved before every question has been answered,” says Jørgen Jørgensen, CEO and fourth-generation owner of Norrøna. “For nearly a century, Norrøna has developed products around the demands of the outdoors. We are now bringing that experience upstream, helping shape the fibre itself around what outdoor performance requires.” Unlike synthetic material that can shed tiny fibres during wear and washing that stay in the environment for a long time, Uluu’s material is designed to biodegrade, passing TUV marine and home biodegradable tests. The process starts with a low-impact raw material, since seaweed is harvested without farmland, minimum freshwater or fertilizer. Fermentation The process works much like a brewery, fermenting sugars from the seaweed in saltwater to create a natural material that can then be made into fibre. articles.o: Independent Apparels partners with Panacea to strengthen skills for a changing RMG sector
articles.s: Rising production costs, energy uncertainty, global competition and changing buyer expectations are putting new demands on Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry. Meeting these challenges requires more than investment in machinery and technology. It also calls for stronger skills, practical knowle
articles.x: Rising production costs, energy uncertainty, global competition and changing buyer expectations are putting new demands on Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry. Meeting these challenges requires more than investment in machinery and technology. It also calls for stronger skills, practical knowledge and the ability to share and apply that knowledge across factory teams. Against this backdrop, Independent Apparels Ltd. has partnered with Panacea Private Consulting Group on a two-year Manufacturing Excellence project. The initiative aims to improve factory performance while building the skills and internal capability needed to sustain improvements over time. The launch was attended by S. M. Abu Tayyab, Managing Director of Independent Apparels; Syed Tanzim Mozaher, Director, Independent Apparels Ltd; Brothers Apparels Ltd; and members of the company’s leadership team. Dr. Azim Mohammad, Managing Director of Panacea, joined the event with the firm’s Vice President, Senior Consultant, and other team members. Improving productivity depends on better work methods, informed decision-making and the ability to identify and solve problems at the factory level. These changes are more likely to last when employees understand new practices, can apply them in their work and share what they learn with colleagues. Knowledge and skills transfer will therefore be an important part of the project. Under the leadership of Mr. Tayyab, Independent Apparels is pursuing improvements across its manufacturing operations. Established in 1997, the company has a longstanding presence in Bangladesh’s apparel industry. The project will create an opportunity to build on that experience while developing new operational and management capabilities. Panacea, one of Bangladesh’s leading consulting orga

articles.x: By: Seshadri Ramkumar, Professor, Texas Tech University, USA (Lubbock, USA, November 04, 2026)— Creating new markets for cotton is a priority for the global cotton sector. Gen Z researchers endeavor to create new cotton products with advanced applications. Global cotton industry is working to enhance its market share by: 1) developing new products such as advanced textiles, 2) engaging with youth population, and 3) improving the quality-cost balance. United States-based Cotton Incorporated is engaged in research and development and marketing to increase the consumption of cotton. Recent research by two undergraduate students in the Nonwovens & Advanced Cotton Laboratory at Texas Tech University, USA utilized plasma surface modification to improve functional and mechanical properties of cotton nonwoven products. The students were from the Departments of Physics and Astronomy and Biology, emphasizing the need to have multidisciplinary approach in developing value-added cotton products. Research at the Nonwovens and Advanced Cotton Laboratory at Texas Tech University focuses on increasing the demand for cotton by developing advanced textiles from cotton and outreach to increase the utility of sustainable products. The laboratory engages with undergraduates and high schools and encourages them in undertaking research on cotton and sustainable materials for functional applications. Plasma treatment used Argon gas to develop stronger oil absorbent cotton nonwovens. Building on earlier research on the application of raw cotton as an absorbent for crude oil, undergraduate students focused on exploring additional functionalities. Gopalakrishnan With nearly three decades of experience and over 300 machines supplied worldwide, InspirOn Engineering continues to develop its Motex stenter range around energy efficiency, process control, fabric versatility and dependable after-sales support. Executive Director Mrs. Radhika Bhagwati discusses the company’s technological strengths, evolving customer requirements and plans for INDIA ITME 2026. InspirOn Engineering has steadily strengthened its position in textile finishing through its Motex range of stenter machines, combining engineering expertise with a focus on productivity, fabric quality and cost-effectiveness. The company’s journey in stenter manufacturing began in 1996 through a joint venture with A.Monforts, Germany. Since then, it has supplied more than 300 machines worldwide. Mrs. Radhika Bhagwati, Executive Director According to Mrs. Radhika Bhagwati, (ED), InspirOn Engineering, three priorities are increasingly shaping product development: sustainability, automation and flexibility. Textile processors require equipment that can handle diverse fabric types, deliver consistent quality and reduce energy consumption without compromising productivity. “Customers expect machines that save energy, handle diverse fabrics and deliver consistent quality , and that’s where Motex has evolved,” she says. articles.x: The emergence of linear block silicone copolymers marked a major paradigm shift in textile finishing, overcoming the performance trade-offs inherent in conventional amino and amido-silicone softeners. By integrating alternating segments of flexible polydimethylsiloxane and amino blocks into a single backbone, this unique architecture maximizes luxurious hand-feel while radically enhancing yellowing resistance and application stability. Unlike traditional silicones that frequently fail under harsh processing conditions, the securely configured functional groups in block silicones withstand high shear, extreme pH, and elevated temperatures. Figure: Edward Menezes, Executive Chairman, Rossari Biotech Ltd. While most standard block copolymers effectively use high-shear homogenization or microemulsification to form oil-in-water emulsions stabilized by suitable surfactants, this approach carries some inherent practical and technical limitations. Process dependency: Achieving and maintaining a fine, stable emulsion particle size depends on emulsification equipment, surfactant selection, and careful process control, both at the manufacturer and, for in-house emulsified products, at the mill. Bath stability issues: Conventional emulsions can be sensitive to electrolytes, hardness, pH swings, and the presence of other anionic or cationic auxiliaries in the finishing bath, increasing the risk of creaming, flocculation, or silicone spotting on fabric. Shelf-life and logistics: Coarser or less robustly stabilized emulsions are more prone to phase separation during storage and transport, particularly across temperature fluctuations. articles.x: By K. Gopalakrishnan Jintex’s Ganesh H.R. explains how A Team is combining Taiwanese machinery, chemistry, automation and process expertise to help Indian manufacturers accelerate their move into MMF, sportswear and technical textiles. India’s textile industry is entering a decisive new phase. The country has built formidable scale and capability in cotton, but the next wave of growth is increasingly being shaped by man-made fibres (MMF), functional textiles, sportswear, athleisure and technical applications. Recognising this shift, Jintex Corporation Ltd. has joined forces with a group of established Taiwanese machinery, automation and textile-technology companies to create A Team—an integrated platform designed to bring Taiwan’s synthetic-textile know-how closer to Indian manufacturers. In an interaction with The Textile Magazine, Ganesh H.R., Senior Vice President – South Asia, Jintex Corporation Ltd., explains why India’s synthetic-textile opportunity is gathering momentum, how A Team was conceived, and why technology must be supported by process knowledge, local service and application expertise if India is to compete successfully in global performance-textile markets. Ganesh H.R., Senior Vice President – South Asia, Jintex Corporation Ltd. India’s Synthetic Opportunity India’s shift towards synthetics has become far more visible over the past three to four years. Jintex had been tracking the segment for more than a decade, but Ganesh says the recent acceleration is materially different in both pace and intent. The structural reason is clear: while India remains strongly cotton-oriented, the global fibre mix is increasingly dominated by synthetics. articles.o: Helping fabrics retain their functional properties
articles.s: New textile finishing technologies introduced by Switzerland’s Sanitized and Germany’s Rudolf are designed to address two factors that can limit the useful life of clothing and technical textiles – persistent odours and declining weather protection. Sanitized has introduced Odorex EON, a biocide-fre
articles.x: New textile finishing technologies introduced by Switzerland’s Sanitized and Germany’s Rudolf are designed to address two factors that can limit the useful life of clothing and technical textiles – persistent odours and declining weather protection. Sanitized has introduced Odorex EON, a biocide-free treatment developed to tackle the accumulation of body oils and odour-causing residues in performance apparel, while Rudolf has launched Ruco-Dry Eco CWS, a water-repellent finish designed to provide improved resistance to rain and moisture, particularly in cotton fabrics. The two companies are highlighting their respective developments as part of a broader approach to textile durability that extends beyond conventional measures such as strength, abrasion resistance and wash performance. One particular challenge for sportswear manufacturers is the persistence of unpleasant odours in synthetic garments, even after repeated laundering. Sometimes referred to as “permastink”, this can result from the gradual accumulation of sebum and other residues within textile fibres. Sanitized Odorex EON employs a dual-action approach intended to address both immediate odours and their longer-term accumulation. During wear, the treatment adsorbs and neutralises odour molecules, while also creating a protective layer that helps release sebum residues during laundering. The aim is to prevent the progressive build-up of contaminants that can make otherwise serviceable garments unpleasant to wear. articles.x: Santoni China Group will participate in ITMA ASIA + CITME 2026 , taking place from November 20–24 at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (NECC) in Shanghai. Under the theme “Machines Evolved · Intelligence Delivered,” the Group will showcase circular and seamless knitting technologies, innovative textile applications, the SWS 3D AI design platform and integrated digital solutions from its brands, including Santoni, Jingmei and Terrot, at Hall 4.1, Booth C39 . Founded in Brescia, Italy, in 1919, Santoni has built a century-long legacy of innovation in knitting technology. Since establishing its manufacturing presence in China in 2005, Santoni China has remained at the forefront of the knitting industry, advancing both circular knitting machinery and the transformative potential of digitalization and artificial intelligence. Today, the Group brings together six distinctive equipment and component brands, four integrated engineering, R&D and manufacturing hubs, and a digital ecosystem designed for intelligent manufacturing. By uniting hardware with software, and specialist expertise with scalable capabilities, Santoni China Group goes beyond creating the machines and technologies that shape the fabrics of tomorrow—it is helping reimagine the future value chain of knitted products. articles.o: Consumption to Exceed Production Based on Resilient Demand in Asia
articles.s: Global cotton consumption is projected to exceed production in the 2026/27 season as output declines across several major producing countries while demand remains relatively stable, according to the November edition of Cotton This Month, published by the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC
articles.x: Global cotton consumption is projected to exceed production in the 2026/27 season as output declines across several major producing countries while demand remains relatively stable, according to the November edition of Cotton This Month , published by the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC). World cotton production is estimated at 25.75 million tonnes, down approximately 4% from 26.85 million tonnes in 2025/26. Global consumption, meanwhile, is projected to increase slightly to 26.10 million tonnes, compared with 25.89 million tonnes the previous season. The projections indicate that consumption will exceed production by approximately 353,000 tonnes, reversing the previous season’s production surplus of nearly 961,000 tonnes. The shift suggests a modest drawdown in global cotton inventories. Production Declines Across Major Suppliers The decline in global production reflects reduced crop prospects in several major cotton-producing countries. China’s production is projected to fall by approximately 4%, from 7.5 million tonnes to 7.2 million tonnes, while Brazil’s output is expected to decline by about 2%, from 4.25 million tonnes to 4.10 million tonnes. Production in Pakistan is also forecast to fall by approximately 17%, while the United States is expected to record a decline of about 4%. India’s production is projected to remain stable at 5.3 million tonnes, while West African output is expected to increase modestly to approximately 954,000 tonnes. The outlook remains subject to weather-related risks, particularly in India and West Africa, where irregular rainfall, drought, excessive moisture, and pest pressure could affect yields and lead to further revisions as the season progresses. articles.s: Three years after its launch in English, Spanish, French and Turkish, Barmag’s Digital Academy online training centre for the BCF process is now also available in Chinese. Available on the e-commerce platform myBarmag.com, it offers a wide range of e-learning modules on the operation, maintenance, a
articles.x: Three years after its launch in English, Spanish, French and Turkish, Barmag’s Digital Academy online training centre for the BCF process is now also available in Chinese. Available on the e-commerce platform myBarmag.com, it offers a wide range of e-learning modules on the operation, maintenance, and repair of the Neumag BCF S+ and S8 systems. The training programme is aimed at operators, process engineers and technicians, as well as quality managers. Compact, role-based learning units, accessible via mobile and desktop devices, allow users to quickly apply the content. At the same time, the programme consistently shares Barmag’s OEM expertise regarding the operation and maintenance of the machines. In contrast to work methods that have evolved individually, all processes are standardised and followed through in complete detail. This ensures that users learn and apply the defined best practices. Progress assessments help participants internalize the contents and reinforce what they have learned and exams and certificates document their learning achievements. Feedback features can quickly clarify comprehension questions at any time. Access to the Digital Academy is granted on a location or company-specific basis. Around 450 active users have already recognised the benefits of Barmag’s digital classroom for themselves. Most of them are based in the US but with the launch of the Chinese version, this service is now accessible to an even larger customer base.
