articles.t: KATRI시험연구원, 방화두건 첫 소방장비인증
articles.o: KATRI시험연구원, 방화두건 첫 소방장비인증
articles.s: KATRI시험연구원(원장 신동준)이 소방장비 업체 위버드의 방화두건에 소방장비인증(KFAC) 섬유류 분야 제1호 인증서를 2026년 10월 발급했다고 밝혔다.KATRI는 소방청으로부터 방화복, 방화두건, 방화장갑, 방화신발 등 4개 품목의 소방장비인증 지정기관으로 인가받아 시험·인증 업무를 수행하고 있다. 이번 인증은 이 가운데 방화두건 품목에 대한 첫 인증이다.방화두건은 화재 진압과 구조 활동 중 소방관의 머리와 목, 안면 부위를 화염과 열기, 이물질로부터 보호하는 개인보호장비다. KATRI는 서류심사와 현장심사, 제품 성능 심사

articles.x: With a broad technology portfolio, continuous innovation and stronger customer engagement in India, DiloGroup is positioning itself to meet evolving demands across the global nonwovens industry. DiloGroup has witnessed a significant increase in demand since mid-2026, translating into a larger order pipeline for major projects across the nonwovens industry. While opportunities span multiple applications rather than any single sector, the company is responding with a comprehensive portfolio of machinery, flexible production technologies and modernisation solutions. Ms. Riccarda Dilo, General Management at DiloGroup For Ms. Riccarda Dilo, General Management at DiloGroup, the priorities are clear: deliver measurable production benefits, help manufacturers adapt to changing requirements and build long-term customer partnerships. India, with its established textile manufacturing base and expanding technical textiles sector, is an important part of this strategy. Innovation That Delivers Measurable Gains DiloGroup’s technology development extends beyond improving individual machine performance. Its focus is on enhancing the complete production process while enabling manufacturers to develop new products and applications. Among the key developments are MicroPunch, 3D-Lofter, IsoFeed VRS and the latest needlelooms, complemented by technologies designed to improve operating efficiency and flexibility. The MODILOUS needle module technology enables faster, more cost-efficient needle changes and needle board cleaning. SuperPunch and PowerPunch address requirements for higher production speeds and very high needling forces. articles.s: What the differing market dynamics mean for members of the Swiss Textile Machinery Association China and India are among the world’s most important textile manufacturing markets and have long been key destinations for Swiss textile machinery. However, their industrial structures, raw material bases
articles.x: What the differing market dynamics mean for members of the Swiss Textile Machinery Association China and India are among the world’s most important textile manufacturing markets and have long been key destinations for Swiss textile machinery. However, their industrial structures, raw material bases and market dynamics differ considerably. These differences create distinct requirements and opportunities for Swiss suppliers of machinery, components and services. With ITMA Asia + CITME in Shanghai and ITME in Greater Noida, India, two major Asian textile machinery exhibitions will take place in late 2026. China and India have extensive textile manufacturing capacities, large domestic markets and significant positions in international textile trade. Both countries are important markets for the Swiss textile machinery industry. Many Swiss companies have established a strong local presence through production facilities, sales and service organizations, reflecting their long-term commitment to these markets. “China and India are both key markets for our industry, but their industrial environments differ notably,” explains Cornelia Buchwalder, Secretary General of Swiss Textile Machinery. “The structure of textile production, the availability of raw materials and the importance of domestic demand all influence their investment priorities. Understanding these differences is essential for our member companies to offer technologies that meet the specific requirements of each market.” China: Technological advancement and strong competition China is by far the world’s largest textile manufacturing country, with an extensive and highly integrated value chain covering virtually every stage of textile production. articles.s: Asahi Kasei’s premium stretch fibre brand Roica is making its debut at Functional Fabric Fair Portland, bringing together textile innovations from European and Asian partners for applications ranging from outdoor performance and cycling to innerwear, athleisure and everyday apparel. articles.x: Asahi Kasei’s premium stretch fibre brand Roica is making its debut at Functional Fabric Fair Portland, bringing together textile innovations from European and Asian partners for applications ranging from outdoor performance and cycling to innerwear, athleisure and everyday apparel. The company is presenting a diverse collection of advanced fabric developments at the Oregon Convention Center on 27-28 October 2026, with its stand 256 showcasing the latest innovations from its global textile partner network. © Sitip | Asahi Kasei Under the brand message ‘Stretch Your Future’, Roica is highlighting how collaboration across the textile supply chain is driving new developments in comfort, fit, functionality and material innovation. The European showcase features textile developments from Borgini Jersey, Brugnoli, Cifra, Penn Solutions, Sitip and Tiba Tricot, demonstrating the versatility of stretch technology across performance and lifestyle applications. © Cifra | Asahi Kasei Highlights include premium athleisure fabrics combining refined aesthetics with a luxurious handle, engineered knitted constructions designed to improve ergonomic comfort, seamless garment technologies and technical fabrics for cycling and other performance applications. The collection also includes three-dimensional mesh structures suitable for apparel, accessories and bags, illustrating the expanding role of engineered stretch fabrics beyond conventional clothing applications. Selected developments incorporate specialised Roica fibres, including Roica EF, which uses pre-consumer recycled yarn waste as part of its raw material input. articles.o: Roaches delivers record lab order to Indonesia
articles.s: Over this summer, Roaches International – a member of the British Textile Machinery Association (BTMA) – has dispatched its largest integrated order for textile laboratory equipment to date. A total of 19 testing machines weighing more than two tons have been delivered for a new lab being establishe
articles.x: Over this summer, Roaches International – a member of the British Textile Machinery Association (BTMA) – has dispatched its largest integrated order for textile laboratory equipment to date. A total of 19 testing machines weighing more than two tons have been delivered for a new lab being established by Indonesia’s Alia Digital Printex, demonstrating the British manufacturer’s ability to supply complete testing facilities rather than just individual instruments. Established in Jakarta in 2017, Alia Digital Printex specialises in digital textile printing and fabric production, particularly for scarves, hijabs, prayer garments and apparel. Employing more than 500 people, it has a printing capacity of 18,000 metres of fabric per day and serves fashion brands in Indonesia and international markets. The new lab will support its expanding manufacturing activities and requirements for consistent fabric quality and performance. Working with its Indonesian partner PT. Kawan Era Baru, Roaches has coordinated the project from design and equipment specification through to manufacturing, dispatch and on-site engineering support. Connected future The order also highlights the advantages of sourcing a complete testing laboratory from a single supplier as textile manufacturers move towards more digitally integrated quality control operations. Looking ahead, artificial intelligence is predicted to accelerate this transition, enabling information from previously independent instruments to be combined and analysed to identify relationships between fabric properties, processing conditions and finished product quality. articles.x: From PCB fiberglass fabrics to denim production, and from premium Jacquard weaving to 3D technical textiles, Stäubli continues to drive Asia's textile industry transformation through innovative technologies. With reliable machine performance, advanced automation solutions, and a comprehensive service offering covering the entire equipment lifecycle, Stäubli is committed to helping weaving mills enhance productivity and overall operational efficiency, enabling them to better meet future market challenges. At ITMA ASIA 2026, Stäubli will exhibit at Booth D05 in Hall 3, showcasing innovative solutions across the entire weaving process. From weaving preparation to advanced shedding systems, including Jacquard technology, and technical weaving systems, Stäubli delivers future-ready intelligent production capabilities designed to support the next generation of Asian weaving manufacturers. Advanced weaving solutions for high-volume Asian production environments In an Asian market shaped by high production volumes, increasing quality expectations, and growing demand for automation and process reliability, weaving mills are looking for technologies that help them improve efficiency, and remain competitive over the long term. Stäubli solutions are designed to help manufacturers achieve stable processes, consistent fabric quality, reduced downtime, and reliable performance across extended production runs. At the booth, visitors will be able to discover technologies that respond directly to the needs of modern weaving mills: faster preparation, precise shedding, flexible patterning, robust operation, and dedicated support throughout the machine lifecycle. articles.t: House of Bruar는 "성숙한 쇼핑객이 소매 기술을 수용함을 증명"하여 디지털 영수증 오픈율 70%를 달성했습니다.
articles.o: House of Bruar “Proves Mature Shoppers Embrace Retail Tech”, Achieving an Exceptional 70% Open Rate on Digital Receipts
articles.s: Known as the "Harrods of the North", the Scottish retailer is challenging industry assumptions by driving a strong engagement rate among its core customer base using Yocuda’s digital receipt solution. The post House of Bruar “Proves Mature Shoppers Embrace Retail Tech”, Achieving an Exceptional 70%
articles.x: Known as the "Harrods of the North", the Scottish retailer is challenging industry assumptions by driving a strong engagement rate among its core customer base using Yocuda’s digital receipt solution. London, 27th October 2026 – House of Bruar, one of Scotland’s leading luxury country lifestyle department stores, has transformed its in-store customer experience with dynamic digital receipts, debunking the assumption that mature shoppers are reluctant to engage with digital retail technology. By partnering with Yocuda , the market leader in dynamic digital receipts, House of Bruar has unlocked impressive post-purchase engagement. Despite initial concerns regarding its mature customer base – the largest visitor age group is 55 to 64 years old – shoppers have actively interacted with the new digital channel. Key Engagement Statistics & Performance Highlights: 70% Open Rate: digital receipts achieved an exceptional 70% open rate, over four times the standard retail marketing email benchmark of 17%. 6% Click-Through Rate: click-through rates reached 6% – nearly nine times the retail industry average of 0.7% – driving store shoppers back to online catalogues, product recommendations, and brand content. articles.x: Italian stretch fabric specialist Carvico is presenting its vision for 2028 at MarediModa in Cannes this week, unveiling a new TrendBook that explores the relationship between colour, materials, garment construction and technical performance. Entitled Not Just to Seduce , the TrendBook introduces five creative directions – Animalia, Manly, Origami, Ornamenta and Bodycon – which demonstrate how different fabric weights, textures and structures can be combined within a unified colour palette. The collection reflects Carvico’s ambition to move beyond conventional beachwear applications, developing a more versatile approach to contemporary clothing in which swimwear, activewear and ready-to-wear increasingly overlap. The presentation demonstrates how contrasting materials, finishes and garment constructions can work together within a single design concept. Central to the approach is the idea that colour can provide a common starting point for combining fabrics with different technical properties and aesthetic characteristics. Bodysuits, bikinis and swimsuits are reinterpreted as versatile wardrobe components that can be worn beyond the beach, alongside jackets, shirts, skirts and trousers. The result is a hybrid approach to clothing that combines technical performance with contemporary fashion design. articles.t: Karl Mayer는 더 미세한 warp 니트 원단을 위해 TM Weft를 업그레이드합니다.
articles.o: Karl Mayer upgrades TM Weft for finer warp-knitted fabrics
articles.s: German textile machinery manufacturer Karl Mayer has upgraded its TM Weft warp knitting machine with an E 36 gauge, an electronic EL pattern drive, and continuous yarn tension regulation. The upgrades...
articles.x: German textile machinery manufacturer Karl Mayer has upgraded its TM Weft warp knitting machine with an E 36 gauge, an electronic EL pattern drive, and continuous yarn tension regulation. The upgrades target finer fabrics, greater design flexibility, and consistent quality for fashion and apparel applications. Figure: Karl Mayer's weft insertion system The company’s new WovenLike collection demonstrates the machine’s potential to produce woven-look fabrics through warp knitting. The lightest fabric weighs 63 grams per square meter, offering potential for lightweight apparel and fashion applications. The E 36 gauge expands the machine’s existing E 24, E 28, and E 32 range. A higher gauge generally supports finer fabric structures, depending on yarn selection and machine configuration. The EL pattern drive expands patterning options, while continuous yarn tension regulation helps maintain consistent yarn processing and fabric quality. The TM Weft platform offers working widths of 215, 247 and 270 inches. Its weft insertion system accommodates 36 ends. The new fabric collection explores different textures and appearances using materials such as acetate, viscose, cotton blends, metallic yarns and stretch fibers. Karl Mayer will present the upgraded machine and fabric collection at ITMA ASIA + CITME 2026 in Shanghai from November 20 to 24. The company has not disclosed quantified gains in production speed, output or energy efficiency from the latest upgrades. For Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry, the development offers another option for exploring lightweight, differentiated fabrics. Commercial adoption will depend on machine investment costs, production performance, and demand for the resulting products.

articles.o: Second life for World Cup graphics
articles.s: All 131 panels used to transform Vancouver’s Science World into a giant football for the 2026 FIFA World Cup are being reused, donated or converted into new products by large-format graphics specialist The Look Company. The Seattle-based company, which engineered and installed the 65,000-square-foot
articles.x: All 131 panels used to transform Vancouver’s Science World into a giant football for the 2026 FIFA World Cup are being reused, donated or converted into new products by large-format graphics specialist The Look Company. The Seattle-based company, which engineered and installed the 65,000-square-foot graphic installation, is transforming much of the recovered material into a limited collection of bags and umbrellas, with proceeds supporting science education programmes across British Columbia. The installation, known as The Beautiful Dome, transformed Vancouver’s Science World into the official match ball of the tournament and became one of its most photographed landmarks. Large-format graphics are frequently designed for a single event and discarded afterwards, but The Look Company planned for the panels to have a second life from the outset. None of the material recovered from the installation is destined for landfill. Removal began in September, four months after the 40-metre installation was completed. The same five-person rope access team which installed the graphics in May dismantled the dome over two weeks, allowing the panels to be recovered intact. Selected panels have been donated to seven institutions across British Columbia, including Science World, BC Place and the Museum of Vancouver. “An installation this size involves thousands of decisions about how something goes together, and every one of those decisions also determines whether it can come apart,” said Jacob Burke, global CEO of The Look Company. “We engineered 131 panels to fit a curved dome. The precision of that design enables us to bring them down clean, sort them and hand them to a museum or a cutting table instead of a landfill. articles.o: PM Tarique Rahman urges Uniqlo to expand investment in Bangladesh
articles.s: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has invited Uniqlo to expand its investment in Bangladesh, with a focus on man-made fiber products, technical textiles, and sustainable apparel manufacturing. The move un...
articles.x: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has invited Uniqlo to expand its investment in Bangladesh, with a focus on man-made fiber products, technical textiles, and sustainable apparel manufacturing. The move underscores Bangladesh’s ambition to diversify its textile sector and strengthen its position in higher-value, innovation-driven exports. The prime minister made the call during a meeting with a delegation led by Tadashi Yanai, chairman, president and chief executive officer of Fast Retailing Co Ltd, Uniqlo’s parent company, in Tokyo. During the meeting, Tarique Rahman appreciated Uniqlo’s confidence in Bangladesh and its longstanding business relationship with the country. He encouraged the company to explore further investment opportunities in the country’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector, with a focus on diversifying production and moving towards higher-value apparel. Discussions covered technology transfer, skills development, product innovation, advanced manufacturing systems and the adoption of environmentally friendly production processes. The prime minister said the government was ready to provide necessary support to facilitate Uniqlo’s business expansion in Bangladesh. Potential assistance includes land allocation, investment approvals and simplified administrative procedures. The proposed investment areas align with Bangladesh’s efforts to diversify its apparel export basket beyond conventional cotton-based products and strengthen its position in higher-value segments of the global textile and apparel market. articles.s: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Department of Textile Engineering of City University and Ha-Meem Group was signed during the visit to its head office in the Tejgaon Industrial Area in Dhaka. The signing of the MoU took place during the visit led by Dr. A K M Saiful Islam (Head of the
articles.x: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Department of Textile Engineering of City University and Ha-Meem Group was signed during the visit to its head office in the Tejgaon Industrial Area in Dhaka. The signing of the MoU took place during the visit led by Dr. A K M Saiful Islam (Head of the Department of Textile Engineering), accompanied by Md. Arifuzzaman (Associate Professor) and Md. Ashnaim Bari (Assistant Professor) on October 27th, 2026. On behalf of Ha-Meem Group, the signing ceremony was attended by Abdullah Al Helal Sarker (Assistant General Manager, Human Resources), Parvez Ahmed (Senior Manager, Human Resources), and Touhedul Islam (Assistant Manager, Human Resources). The purpose of this MoU is to establish a framework for academic–industry collaboration between the Department of Textile Engineering, City University and Ha-Meem Group to enhance practical learning, industrial exposure, professional development, research collaboration, and knowledge exchange in the field of textile engineering and related disciplines. Ha-Meem Group stands as one of the leading conglomerates and key players in Bangladesh’s global apparel supply chain. Through this partnership, students will gain comprehensive industrial exposure, structured internship pathways, technical training, joint research opportunities, and direct employment linkages. This bridge between academic curriculum and operational reality aims to address prevailing skill gaps at a pivotal time, as the ready-made garment (RMG) sector undergoes rapid technological innovation, automation, sustainability, and AI-driven transformation. BEMACID Brilliant Blue F-WN: Brilliant Blue for Polyamide and Wool With BEMACID Brilliant Blue F-WN, the CHT Group is expanding its BEMACID F portfolio with a highly brilliant blue dye designed for polyamide and wool applications. The dye is also metal-free and AOX-free, offering important formulation benefits for modern textile processing. For dyers and textile manufacturers working with polyamide and wool, color intensity, fastness performance, and process reliability are essential to producing competitive textile products. BEMACID Brilliant Blue F-WN adds a versatile blue component to the CHT Group’s portfolio, helping manufacturers meet these requirements. BEZAKTIV Solar Yellow ONE: Flexibility for Modern Dyeing Processes With BEZAKTIV Solar Yellow ONE, the CHT Group is strengthening its high-performance reactive dyes portfolio with a lightfast, non-photochromic golden yellow dye. It delivers reliable, uniform dyeing results across a broad range of color depths, from light to deep shades. The product offers very good wash-off properties and is suitable for both exhaust and continuous dyeing processes, providing flexibility for different production requirements. BEZAKTIV Solar Yellow ONE can also be used effectively in trichromatic dyeing systems alongside BEZAKTIV Coral Red ONE and BEZAKTIV Aquamarine ONE. articles.s: AI로 제작한 테니스 착장 콘텐츠가 미국 브랜드의 승인을 받아 화제를 모으고 있다. 이를 발판으로 국내 원단을 활용한 제품화에도 도전한다.부천대학교 섬유패션디자인학과 학생들이 미국 패션 브랜드 배들리 미슈카(Badgley Mischka)와 손잡고 AI 기반 패션 콘텐츠 제작과 의류 디자인 개발에 도전, 글로벌 브랜드 협업 성과를 선보였다. 실제 브랜드의 의류 샘플을 바탕으로 AI 홍보 콘텐츠를 제작해 브랜드 측의 승인을 받은 데 이어, 국내 원단을 활용한 독자적인 디자인 제품 개발까지 추진하며 디지털 기술과 패션 실무를 연결했다.정

articles.o: Primark joins Denim Deal to scale recycled cotton in jeans
articles.s: Primark has joined the Denim Deal, a global industry initiative aimed at increasing the use of post-consumer recycled cotton in denim and improving circularity across the fashion supply chain. Figure...
articles.x: Primark has joined the Denim Deal, a global industry initiative aimed at increasing the use of post-consumer recycled cotton in denim and improving circularity across the fashion supply chain. Figure:Primark’s Circular Product Standard focuses on three principles: durability, the use of recycled or more sustainably sourced materials, and recyclability. Announced on October 27, 2026, the partnership brings together brands, manufacturers, suppliers and recyclers to address technical and sourcing challenges that limit the wider use of recycled cotton in jeans. According to Primark, the collaboration will provide access to industry expertise, technical support and joint research and development opportunities. The move builds on the retailer’s first reclaimed denim collection, launched in February 2026. The five-piece collection covers womenswear and menswear, with each product containing at least 20% recycled denim made from discarded textiles. The remaining cotton comes from Primark’s Cotton Project, which supports cotton farmers in its supply chain. The collection was designed to improve recyclability by removing stretch and unnecessary metal components, including rivets, and using recyclable trims. These design choices aim to make garments easier to process when they reach the end of their useful life. According to Primark, 8% of its denim units sold in the 2024/25 financial year met its circular-by-design criteria. Across all clothing categories, the share was 5%. Primark’s Circular Product Standard focuses on three principles: durability, the use of recycled or more sustainably sourced materials, and recyclability. articles.o: Hygienix 2026 award finalists announced
articles.s: Four innovations have now been shortlisted for the 2026 Hygienix Innovation Award. The finalists, announced by nonwovens association INDA, are Anabio Technologies, Confitex Technology, The Lycra Company and Youth Crews. Each will present its development at Hygienix 2026, taking place from November 1
articles.x: Four innovations have now been shortlisted for the 2026 Hygienix Innovation Award. The finalists, announced by nonwovens association INDA, are Anabio Technologies, Confitex Technology, The Lycra Company and Youth Crews. Each will present its development at Hygienix 2026, taking place from November 16-19th at the Hyatt Regency Houston in Texas, with the winner announced on the final day. Anabio Technologies has developed a patented flushable sanitary pad designed to address the persistent waste problem associated with conventional menstrual products, which can take hundreds of years to break down. Its multilayer construction provides up to 12 hours of protection before dispersing when flushed. The product has been independently tested against International Water Services Flushability Group (IWSFG) requirements and is designed for use with flush toilets, septic systems and pit latrines. Importantly, it can also be manufactured on conventional converting lines, potentially easing its transition to commercial production. Confitex Technology, which won last year’s award for its washable nonwoven sanitary pad, is extending its reusable absorbent technology into the automotive market with washable nonwoven car seat protectors. Manufactured entirely from nonwoven materials, the protectors incorporate a patented leak-resistant structure capable of absorbing and retaining up to 700 ml of liquid. Independent testing has also verified their continued performance after more than 30 washes. The development represents a potentially significant new application for washable nonwoven absorbent products beyond conventional personal hygiene. articles.o: EOA, ‘풀써마 프로’ CJ온스타일 첫 방송 준비 물량 소진
articles.s: 더퓨처의 뷰티 브랜드 EOA가 홈케어 디바이스 ‘풀써마 프로’의 CJ온스타일 첫 방송에서 준비 물량이 모두 소진됐다고 밝혔다. EOA는 오는 11월 8일 낮 12시 25분 후속 방송을 진행하고 유통 채널을 통한 고객 접점을 확대할 계획이다.EOA는 지난 24일 70분간 진행된 방송에서 풀써마 프로와 ‘콜라겐 시너지 부스팅 젤’ 2개로 구성한 기획세트를 선보였다. 회사 측은 방송에 준비한 수량이 모두 소진됐다고 설명했으며, 구체적인 준비 수량은 공개하지 않았다.풀써마 프로는 6.78㎒ 고주파(RF)를 적용한 가정용 피부 관리 기기다.

articles.t: 총리, Uniqlo에 Bangladesh 투자 확대 촉구
articles.o: PM urges Uniqlo to expand investment in Bangladesh
articles.s: Prime minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday urged Japanese apparel retailer Uniqlo to expand its investment in Bangladesh, particularly in man-made fibres, technical textiles and sustainable garment production. The prime minister made the call during a meeting with a delegation led by Tadashi Yanai,
articles.x: Prime minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday urged Japanese apparel retailer Uniqlo to expand its investment in Bangladesh, particularly in man-made fibres, technical textiles and sustainable garment production. The prime minister made the call during a meeting with a delegation led by Tadashi Yanai, chairman, president and chief executive officer of Fast Retailing Co Ltd, the parent company of Uniqlo, at 10:30am Japan Standard Time in Tokyo . During the meeting, Tarique Rahman appreciated Uniqlo’s confidence in Bangladesh and its long-standing business relationship with the country. He called on the company to explore further investment opportunities in the ready-made garment sector, particularly in the production of man-made fibre-based products, technical textiles and sustainable apparel. The discussions also covered technology transfer, skills development, product innovation, advanced manufacturing systems and the adoption of environmentally friendly production processes. The prime minister said the government was ready to provide the necessary support to facilitate the expansion of Uniqlo’s operations in Bangladesh, including assistance with land allocation, investment approvals and the simplification of administrative procedures. Both sides also emphasised the importance of implementing a Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement, expressing the expectation that it would help expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. Those present at the meeting from the Bangladeshi side included finance and planning minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, prime minister’s adviser on finance and planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir, Invest Bangladesh chairman Ashik Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank governor Md Mostakur R

articles.s: The South India Textile Research Association (SITRA) and the Taiwan Textile Research Institute (TTRI) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to promote research and technical cooperation in key areas of… The post SITRA and TTRI Sign MoU to Advance Textile Research, Innovation and Sustainable Tec
articles.x: The South India Textile Research Association (SITRA) and the Taiwan Textile Research Institute (TTRI) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to promote research and technical cooperation in key areas of textile innovation and technology development. The MoU was signed during the Taipei Innovative Textile Application Show (TITAS) 2026, held in Taiwan from October 6 to 8, 2026. Mr. G. Raj Kumar, Vice Chairman of SITRA, signed the agreement on behalf of SITRA, while Mr. Chiu Sheng-fu, Vice President of TTRI, signed on behalf of TTRI. Industry leaders from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) were present at the signing ceremony, underscoring the importance of international collaboration in advancing textile research and technical capabilities. The collaboration will focus on the development of man-made fibres for speciality applications, medical textiles, and sustainable solutions for the textile processing industry. These priority areas offer opportunities to develop advanced textile products and resource-efficient processes that address emerging industrial and societal needs. The partnership brings together SITRA’s strengths in textile research, testing, consultancy, training and industry support with TTRI’s expertise in advanced textile technologies, applied research and innovation. It aims to translate shared knowledge and research capabilities into practical, scalable solutions for the textile industry. Speaking on the occasion, Mr. G. articles.o: Recover calls for focus on current recycling solutions
articles.s: MADRID – Spanish company Recover has launched a global campaign to promote existing commercial textile recycling solutions. The business argues that industry attention should extend beyond future recycling technologies. Recover notes that its recycled fibres were used in more than 200 million garmen
articles.x: MADRID – Spanish company Recover has launched a global campaign to promote existing commercial textile recycling solutions. The business argues that industry attention should extend beyond future recycling technologies. Recover notes that its recycled fibres were used in more than 200 million garments in 2025. The Spanish recycler said its “REAL. Today, Not Someday” campaign aims to shift some of the sustainability debate towards solutions already operating at scale, alongside investment in emerging technologies. The campaign will run across industry events, trade media and digital channels during the fourth quarter. Recover said its recycled cotton is used in global supply chains and supported by certification, traceability systems and environmental data. Recover’s campaign comes as textile-to-textile recycling continues to face questions over feedstock and the economics of scaling production. “Our industry spends a lot of time talking about what sustainability could look like in five or ten years,” said Boris Mercier, CMO at Recover. “That conversation is important. But so is recognising the solutions that are already available today. REAL is our call to shift some of the attention from future possibilities to present realities. Recover recycled cotton is already proven, already scaled and already being used in hundreds of millions of garments. If we want faster progress, we need both future innovation and real world execution.” Recover says its recycled cotton is made from verified textile waste and that its traceability combines Global Recycled Standard certification with physical and digital tracers. articles.x: A custom-built 5-beam SSMMS line supports Manjushree Spntek’s plans for lightweight hygiene nonwoven fabrics and high performance specialised fabrics. Behind the installation is a team effort linking customer requirements with detailed engineering, manufacturing experience and product development. By Nithin Kumar Forty weeks: the time it takes to bring new life into the world—and the time Manjushree Spntek took to bring its new 5-beam SSMMS line from order to production. Installed within the company’s existing facility in Bidadi Industrial Area near Bengaluru, the line is the result of a finely tuned collaboration between senior management, engineering, production and process teams, QA and NPD, and the machinery supplier. Together, they turned a complex installation into a milestone achievement—one that opens new possibilities in lightweight hygiene fabrics and specialised nonwovens. The new line is in response to its customers who ask for more from their input materials. Softer fabrics must still perform reliably, while lighter constructions must retain the strength required by the finished application. Both must be commercially practical. These requirements shaped the decision to invest and build up the specifications for the new line. For Mr. Rajat Kumar Kedia, Managing Director of Manjushree Spntek, the contribution of the people behind the project is central to its significance. “Our teams across engineering, production, quality and technical functions worked closely throughout the process,” he says. He credits that work with strengthening the company’s internal expertise and deepening its understanding of the machinery and the products it can develop. articles.s: Recover™, a Spanish textile recycling company, has launched its first global brand campaign to accelerate the commercial adoption of recycled cotton. The campaign, titled “REAL. Today, Not Someday.”,...
articles.x: Recover™, a Spanish textile recycling company, has launched its first global brand campaign to accelerate the commercial adoption of recycled cotton. The campaign, titled “REAL. Today, Not Someday.” , will run through the fourth quarter of 2026 across industry events, print, digital channels, and targeted activations. It aims to encourage fashion brands to adopt commercially available recycled cotton while continuing to invest in emerging recycling technologies. According to Recover™, its recycled cotton was used in more than 200 million garments in 2025. The company says its five production hubs across Europe, South Asia, Southeast Asia and Central America provide annual fiber production capacity of 84,300 metric tons. The scale of existing production highlights the gap between commercial availability and wider industry adoption. According to Textile Exchange’s Materials Market Report 2025 , mechanically recycled cotton production reached an estimated 0.3 million tons in 2024, compared with approximately 24.1 million tons of virgin cotton. Recycled cotton therefore represented only about 1% of global cotton production. However, available recycling capacity does not automatically translate into higher recycled content in finished garments. According to Fashion for Good’s October 2026 Cotton Reloop Matrix initiative, mechanical recycling shortens and weakens cotton fibers during processing. Only around 45–50% of the original input typically remains as usable fiber, while the shorter fibers can limit yarn strength and fabric durability. As a result, many commercially available yarns contain around 10% recycled cotton. articles.o: Dhakai Muslin reborn for global luxury markets
articles.s: Bangladesh is reviving its iconic Dhakai muslin through genomic research and traditional craftsmanship. The initiative is empowering rural women artisans and paving the way for the fabric’s return to...
articles.x: Bangladesh is reviving its iconic Dhakai muslin through genomic research and traditional craftsmanship. The initiative is empowering rural women artisans and paving the way for the fabric’s return to global luxury markets. Once prized by Roman, Greek and Arab elites and associated with Mughal royalty, Dhakai muslin is progressing from a research project towards commercial production. The initiative aims to restore traditional craftsmanship, expand cotton cultivation and establish a high-value export industry beyond Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector. The revival initiative began in 2014, when the Bangladesh Handloom Board formed a research team to restore traditional muslin production. Researchers collected 39 wild cotton varieties from areas including Kapasia in Gazipur, Baghabari and Rajshahi, using historical references and illustrations to guide their work. Through DNA sequencing and genomic comparisons with historical muslin samples preserved at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, researchers identified and cultivated Phuti karpas , the indigenous cotton variety associated with traditional Dhakai muslin. The disappearance of this cotton, historically grown in the Meghna River basin, had been a major obstacle to restoring the fabric. Researchers also had to recreate more than 50 specialized tools used in traditional muslin production. Dhakai muslin was renowned for its transparency, lightness and delicate texture. Its varieties included Ab-e-Rawan, meaning flowing water, and Shabnam, meaning morning dew. Malmal Khas was among the most prestigious varieties, associated with Mughal royal attire. articles.o: Study calls for stronger policies to scale textile-to-textile recycling in South Korea
articles.s: South Korea needs stronger policies to turn textile waste into high-value recycled fibers instead of relying on incineration, landfills, and low-value recovery, according to a study published in Scien...
articles.x: South Korea needs stronger policies to turn textile waste into high-value recycled fibers instead of relying on incineration, landfills, and low-value recovery, according to a study published in Scientific Reports on October 26, 2026. The study compared South Korea’s textile waste policies with those of France, the Netherlands, Hungary, Latvia, Germany, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. It found that European frameworks generally cover more stages of the textile life cycle and use economic incentives and public communication measures that were not identified in South Korea’s system. The research highlights a key gap in textile circularity. Recycling technology alone cannot establish a circular supply chain without effective collection, sorting, product design, and market demand for recycled materials. The researchers recommend introducing extended producer responsibility (EPR), designing products for recyclability, tracking materials through digital product passports (DPPs), improving waste sorting, and setting recycled-content requirements. Financial incentives could also help businesses invest in recycling infrastructure. The study’s analysis of recycled products found that selected recycling pathways can process suitable textile waste. However, wider implementation requires improvements in both policy and technology. For textile manufacturers, the findings underline the importance of connecting waste collection and processing with the production of reusable fibers. High-value fiber-to-fiber recycling can retain more material value than disposal or low-value recovery, although the best route depends on fiber composition, product quality, and processing requirements.

articles.x: Engr. Sheikh Toffazzal Hossain, Head of Sales & Marketing at Sirajganj Economic Zone Ltd. (SEZL), visited the Sirajganj Chamber of Commerce & Industry, where he held a constructive discussion with it’s President, Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman Bacchu. The discussion focused on the development and investment opportunities of Sirajganj Economic Zone, with particular emphasis on engaging local entrepreneurs and attracting potential investors from Sirajganj. The meeting also highlighted the importance of collaboration between SEZL and the local business community in promoting industrial growth and creating new opportunities for investment. Mr. Md. Saidur Rahman Bacchu expressed his willingness to support SEZL in connecting with local investors and extending cooperation for the upcoming Sirajganj Investors Roadshow, an initiative aimed at bringing potential investors closer to the opportunities offered by the economic zone. Sirajganj Economic Zone Ltd. remains committed to building strong partnerships with local business leaders, encouraging industrial investment, and contributing to the economic development of Sirajganj and Bangladesh. articles.o: Bio-based Lycra and polyamide in new cycling fabric
articles.s: Brugnoli, The Lycra Company and Italian cycling apparel specialist Pissei have collaborated on a new high-performance fabric containing 89% bio-based materials, as part of a pilot project exploring more sustainable cycling apparel. The PaceSetter project has resulted in a cycling kit comprising shor
articles.x: Brugnoli, The Lycra Company and Italian cycling apparel specialist Pissei have collaborated on a new high-performance fabric containing 89% bio-based materials, as part of a pilot project exploring more sustainable cycling apparel. The PaceSetter project has resulted in a cycling kit comprising shorts and a jersey made from fabrics developed by Brugnoli, with the shorts incorporating its new Br4/E1 material. The fabric combines EVO bio-based polyamide from Italian manufacturer Fulgar, derived from castor beans and corn, with the new Renewable Lycra elastane developed by The Lycra Company, which contains 70% bio-derived content sourced from industrial corn. Together, the two fibres enable Brugnoli to achieve 89% bio-based content in a technical fabric designed to meet the demanding performance requirements of competitive cycling. Br4/E1 is the latest development of Brugnoli’s patented Br4 technology, introduced more than a decade ago to combine high-performance stretch fabrics with reduced environmental impact. The company reports that its proprietary dyeing and finishing technology reduces water and energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional production methods. According to Brugnoli, the bio-based raw materials also offer a reduction of up to 45% in climate change impact compared to conventional fibres, although this figure relates to the materials rather than the complete finished garment. The new fabric has been engineered to provide high compression, muscle support and freedom of movement, while offering improved breathability and odour control. These properties build on Brugnoli’s existing Explosive Technology. What is your strategic vision for the company, and how do you see its role evolving in the next five years? Dhirendra Singh Gautam: Archroma is a globally diversified provider of specialty chemicals serving the textiles, paper, packaging, and coatings industries. articles.o: ShinWon integrates global apparel operations
articles.s: South Korean apparel manufacturer ShinWon Corporation has introduced Sphere, a new integrated enterprise resource planning (ERP) system designed to connect its global manufacturing operations, improve data management and provide a foundation for the wider adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). Sp
articles.x: South Korean apparel manufacturer ShinWon Corporation has introduced Sphere, a new integrated enterprise resource planning (ERP) system designed to connect its global manufacturing operations, improve data management and provide a foundation for the wider adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). Sphere integrates key business systems including product lifecycle management (PLM), supplier relationship management (SRM), manufacturing execution (MES), e-accounting and SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC). The platform connects the entire apparel manufacturing process, from order management and sample development to costing, sourcing, procurement, production, logistics, shipment and settlement. By consolidating workflows and data previously managed through spreadsheets, emails and standalone applications, ShinWon has established standardised business processes across its operations. The system also improves data consistency and accessibility at the product level, enabling the more systematic management of bills of materials (BOM) and production processes for individual garment styles. The integration of sales, product development, procurement, production, logistics and financial data provides a common operational framework across ShinWon’s headquarters and overseas manufacturing subsidiaries, allowing the company to follow consistent processes and data standards. In particular, connecting MES with ERP enables the company to manage production status and costs more effectively, while identifying and responding to manufacturing issues more quickly. Sphere also strengthens ShinWon’s business intelligence capabilities. articles.o: Textile recycling innovation turns retired fire uniforms into new fashion yarns
articles.s: Textile recycling innovation is turning discarded garments into valuable raw materials. A pilot project at RMIT University in Australia is transforming retired Western Australian fire-service uniforms...
articles.x: Textile recycling innovation is turning discarded garments into valuable raw materials. A pilot project at RMIT University in Australia is transforming retired Western Australian fire-service uniforms into new yarns and fashion garments. Figure: Less than 1% of global fiber production came from textile-to-textile recycling in 2023. The project, called Walking in Circles , is led by researcher Lisa Piller. It combines recovered technical fibers from used uniforms with cotton grown in Western Australia’s Kimberley region. The project demonstrates how textile waste can support new product development and local circular production. According to the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), the world generates around 92 million tons of textile waste annually. Less than 1% of global fiber production came from textile-to-textile recycling in 2023. This gap highlights the need for technologies that can recover fibers from used garments and return them to production. Recycling technical textiles can be challenging because of blended fibers, chemical finishes, and demanding material performance requirements. Bangladesh is also exploring ways to turn textile waste into commercial products. A pilot involving UNIDO, Circ, Lenzing, and industry partners processed 2.6 tons of cotton-polyester waste from Fakir Knitwear. The project recovered cotton and polyester for new applications. H&M subsequently used recycled materials from the initiative in commercial products, demonstrating how factory waste can become a resource for global fashion supply chains. For Bangladesh, such innovation could reduce production waste, create additional value from factory scraps, and help manufacturers meet brands’ growing demand for circular materials. articles.x: Australian renewable energy companies are eyeing business opportunities and potential partnerships in Bangladesh to expand cooperation in clean energy technologies, battery energy storage and decarbonisation amid the country’s energy crisis and challenges in securing fossil fuels. Speaking at a seminar titled ‘Renewable Energy, Decarbonisation and Energy Transition’ at a hotel in Dhaka on Monday, Australian Trade and Investment Commissioner for South Asia Murray Spence said Bangladesh offered opportunities for Australian clean energy companies. ‘We have the technology, system know-how and experience that Bangladesh can benefit from,’ he said, adding that Australian companies could work with Bangladeshi firms through licensing agreements, joint ventures and other commercial arrangements. A visiting Australian trade delegation, comprising mainly small and medium-sized enterprises and mid-market companies, presented renewable energy products, services and technologies with potential applications in Bangladesh. The delegation brings together a diverse mix of Australian exporters offering energy and battery storage systems, solar solutions, renewable-powered water solutions for remote areas, solar photovoltaic systems, renewable energy training, hydrogen technology, energy simulation, energy technology, solar installation, clean technology and artificial intelligence solutions. Discussions focused on investment opportunities, financing mechanisms, regulatory frameworks and ways to accelerate clean energy projects in Bangladesh. Participants exchanged views on market-entry opportunities, technology suitability, local partnership models, project financing challenges and regulatory requirements. articles.o: Dornbirn GFC moves dates
articles.s: The 66th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress (GFC) will take place from September 14-16th 2027 in Dornbirn, Austria, moving forward by a day to accommodate ITMA 2027 in Hanover, Germany, which takes place the same week. For the first time, the two major international textile industry events will coincide
articles.x: The 66th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress (GFC) will take place from September 14-16th 2027 in Dornbirn, Austria, moving forward by a day to accommodate ITMA 2027 in Hanover, Germany, which takes place the same week. For the first time, the two major international textile industry events will coincide, offering delegates the opportunity to attend both. While Dornbirn GFC focuses on fibre innovations, scientific research and emerging developments, ITMA showcases the latest textile and apparel manufacturing technologies. The organisers believe the timing will create additional opportunities for international networking and knowledge exchange, bringing together research, materials development and industrial applications. Five key themes Dornbirn GFC 2027 will focus on five principal themes, ranging from fibre innovations and new material developments to the circular economy and advances in recycling technologies. Developments in nonwovens, paper and pulp will also feature prominently, alongside new processing technologies for spinning, weaving and finishing. The fifth theme will address protective clothing. A particular emphasis will be placed on translating scientific research into practical industrial applications, strengthening collaboration between research institutions and manufacturers. Call for papers The call for papers for Dornbirn GFC 2027 will open in mid-November 2026, inviting researchers, developers and industry specialists to submit presentations covering new scientific findings, technological advances and practical innovations. The organisers are particularly interested in contributions demonstrating industrial relevance and encouraging dialogue between research and industry. articles.o: Health benefits with bacteria-derived cellulose
articles.s: Researchers at Spain’s Aimplas Plastics Technology Centre are investigating the use of bacterial cellulose to produce biodegradable cosmetic facial masks capable of delivering active skincare ingredients, with potential applications extending to wound dressings and tissue regeneration. Unlike conven
articles.x: Researchers at Spain’s Aimplas Plastics Technology Centre are investigating the use of bacterial cellulose to produce biodegradable cosmetic facial masks capable of delivering active skincare ingredients, with potential applications extending to wound dressings and tissue regeneration. Unlike conventional cellulose extracted from plants, bacterial cellulose is produced directly by microorganisms through fermentation. Certain bacteria, particularly those belonging to the Komagataeibacter genus, generate a three-dimensional network of extremely fine cellulose nanofibrils as they grow, creating a flexible, highly absorbent material. These bacteria are commonly associated with fermentation processes used to produce vinegar, kombucha and nata de coco. The resulting cellulose has an exceptionally high capacity to absorb and retain water, while its flexibility allows it to conform closely to the contours of the skin. Aimplas is exploring these characteristics in the development of bio-based hydrogel facial masks that can carry active ingredients for skin hydration and recovery following sun exposure. “Bacterial cellulose has very interesting properties for the development of more sustainable, high-performance cosmetic products,” says María José de Manuel, biotechnology researcher at Aimplas. “Its extraordinary water-retention capacity, together with its flexibility and ability to adapt to the skin, make it an ideal material for facial masks and as a support for incorporating cosmetic active ingredients.” Beyond cosmetics The same properties offer opportunities in medical applications, particularly in wound management. articles.o: Integrated textile recycling plant opens in Italy
articles.s: A new €8 million textile recycling plant in northern Italy is combining automated sorting, mechanical fibre recovery and digital traceability in a single industrial process. Opened on September 21st in San Pietro Mosezzo, near Novara, the facility has been developed by Italian recycling company Iger
articles.x: A new €8 million textile recycling plant in northern Italy is combining automated sorting, mechanical fibre recovery and digital traceability in a single industrial process. Opened on September 21st in San Pietro Mosezzo, near Novara, the facility has been developed by Italian recycling company Igers, with German sorting technology specialist Stadler acting as its engineering and technology partner. The plant processes both post-consumer and post-industrial textile waste, converting it into recovered fibres and shredded materials suitable for further processing by the spinning industry. According to the companies, it is the first facility in Italy to integrate all the main stages of textile recycling within a single operation, from initial sorting and sanitisation through to mechanical fibre recovery. The facility has a processing capacity of four tons per hour and represents an investment of approximately €8 million, including €1.3 million in co-financing from Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Its opening comes as the European textile industry faces growing pressure to develop industrial-scale recycling infrastructure, following the introduction of mandatory separate textile waste collection and new extended producer responsibility requirements. Integrated processing At the heart of the facility is a patented process developed by Igers that combines the removal of contaminants, automated material identification and separation, mechanical recycling and digital traceability. The collaboration centres on
articles.x: Italian textile manufacturer Brugnoli has joined forces with The Lycra Company and premium cycling apparel brand Pissei to launch PaceSetter, a project demonstrating how bio-based materials can deliver the demanding technical performance required in professional cycling. The collaboration centres on Brugnoli’s new Br4/E1 fabric, which combines EVO bio-based polyamide from Fulgar with the recently developed Renewable Lycra fibre. The resulting fabric contains 89% bio-based materials while offering high compression, muscle support, comfort and freedom of movement. Developed using Brugnoli’s internationally patented Br4 technology, the fabric also benefits from a production process that reduces water and energy consumption during dyeing and finishing by 20% compared with conventional methods. The new Br4/E1 fabric combines EVO polyamide, derived entirely from renewable castor and corn feedstocks, with Renewable Lycra elastane, which contains 70% bio-derived content sourced from industrial corn. According to the companies, the materials offer the potential to reduce climate change impact by up to 45% compared with conventional alternatives. The Renewable Lycra fibre used in the project is a bio-based version of Lycra Xtra Life, a technology recognised for its durability and resistance to degradation. articles.o: Global activewear brands turn to smart fabrics for cooling, comfort, and performance
articles.s: Global activewear is moving beyond conventional sportswear. Global brands and textile developers use smart fabrics, advanced material engineering, and wearable electronics to improve comfort, safety,...
articles.x: Global activewear is moving beyond conventional sportswear. Global brands and textile developers use smart fabrics, advanced material engineering, and wearable electronics to improve comfort, safety, and athletic performance. Figure: According to Grand View Research, the global smart clothing market is projected to increase from $7.4 billion in 2026 to $38.9 billion by 2033. Courtesy: Collected From fabrics that increase airflow in hot conditions to garments that monitor body movement, textile innovation is responding to changing consumer expectations. People increasingly want clothing that does more than cover the body. They want products that help regulate temperature, manage moisture, support physical activity, and provide useful performance data. According to Grand View Research, the global smart clothing market is projected to increase from $7.4 billion in 2026 to $38.9 billion by 2033, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 26.8%. The forecast reflects growing interest in connected apparel, wearable health monitoring, and advanced textile technologies. Brands focus on functional fabric innovation across two distinct tracks. Passive smart materials react to environmental stimuli without external power sources, as Nike illustrated when it introduced Aero-FIT performance cooling technology in October 2025 to channel more than twice the airflow of legacy athletic apparel through specialized knit structures and fiber geometry. Crafted entirely from textile waste as Nike's first elite performance garment, Aero-FIT highlights how circularity merges with advanced material engineering. Alongside structural venting, passive innovations incorporate phase-change materials and advanced hydrophilic-hydrophobic yarn configurations to accelerate moisture management.

articles.o: Interview of H.E. Mr. Reto Renggli, Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh, with Textile Today
articles.s: This exclusive interview with H.E. Mr. Reto Renggli, Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh, was conducted via email correspondence by Enamul Hafiz Latifee, Chief Research Officer, Textile Today. Tex...
articles.x: This exclusive interview with H.E. Mr. Reto Renggli, Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh, was conducted via email correspondence by Enamul Hafiz Latifee, Chief Research Officer, Textile Today. Textile Today: How do you assess the present state and future direction of Bangladesh–Switzerland trade and investment relations, particularly in textiles and apparel? His Excellency: Thank you for your interest in this topic. As you know, Switzerland has been a longstanding development and economic partner of Bangladesh. Currently, trade and investment relations are a priority topic on our bilateral agenda. In fact, when Switzerland and Bangladesh held the sixth round of bilateral political consultations in June this year in Dhaka, we discussed how the private sectors of both countries can engage more closely. Figure: H.E. Mr. Reto Renggli, Ambassador of Switzerland to Bangladesh. According to Swiss official statistics, Switzerland is a market of more than a billion dollars for Bangladeshi exports. In 2025, our total bilateral trade stood at $1.26 billion, of which Bangladeshi exports to Switzerland were around $1.16 billion, mostly garment products. This figure is remarkable, considering my country has fewer than nine million inhabitants. On the other hand, Bangladesh’s key imports from Switzerland include capital machinery and industrial raw materials, most of which go into the garment sector. Swiss commodity companies are also playing an important role in the textile and apparel industry in this country. These facts not only point to our growing trade exchanges but also indicate the potential they hold, particularly in the textile and apparel industries. articles.s: We still do not know why a senior merchandiser died last week; however, the account he gave his family the night before paints a picture of a workplace atmosphere thousands of textile professionals will recognize. Prof. Md. Masum, PhD On the morning of 14 October, Md Jamal Uddin, who was a senior me
articles.x: We still do not know why a senior merchandiser died last week; however, the account he gave his family the night before paints a picture of a workplace atmosphere thousands of textile professionals will recognize. Prof. Md. Masum, PhD On the morning of 14 October, Md Jamal Uddin, who was a senior merchandiser at a garment factory in Ashulia, died following a fall from the roof of the factory building. According to the police, The Daily Star, the CCTV footage indicates that he committed suicide. However, his family disapproves of this explanation, claims that he was murdered and says the factory is hiding the truth about what took place. Although the factory authorities showed the footage to local journalists, they refused to issue an official statement. His wife said he phoned her the night before; he said there had been trouble at the factory and that he feared the office would implicate him if he didn’t go to work. We have no idea why Jamal Uddin died, and it isn’t appropriate for a newspaper column to come to a conclusion. The task should be left to a thorough and independent inquiry, one that his family is entitled to and which the industry ought to welcome rather than oppose. Until such an inquiry is completed, nobody should say they know the cause. One point in the family’s version of events ought to raise concern among all those working in the textile industry. A senior official, who had access to buyers, orders, and deadlines, allegedly feared that by remaining at home he would appear guilty. In a company with fair procedures, a suspected employee knows exactly what he is being accused of, who will hear his case, and how he can respond. A chemical engineer by training, he brings around 30 years of experience in specialty chemicals and related industries. His career includes senior roles at Unilever and Lenzing
articles.x: ZURICH — October 7, 2026 — Stephan Sielaff took over as Chief Executive Officer of the Schill+Seilacher Group on October 1. A chemical engineer by training, he brings around 30 years of experience in specialty chemicals and related industries. His career includes senior roles at Unilever and Lenzing AG, and most recently at SSI SCHÄFER Plastics. At Schill+Seilacher, Sielaff will lead the next phase of development for the internationally active specialty chemicals Group. Stephan Sielaff For manufacturers and processors of man-made fibers, the Group offers high-performance process auxiliaries for staple fibers and continuous filaments, as well as solutions for the targeted functionalization of nonwovens. Tailored spinning finishes support reliable, efficient processing while giving fibers the specific properties required for their end use – from a pleasantly soft handle to controlled water absorption or repellency. The result is a broad range of solutions designed for diverse requirements and applications, from apparel and hygiene products to technical uses in mobility, construction and infrastructure. For Sielaff, this business exemplifies one of the key strengths of successful specialty chemicals companies: combining decades of experience with the ability to keep adapting to new requirements. “Tradition becomes a competitive advantage in specialty chemicals when experience is continuously translated into new solutions. Schill+Seilacher has extensive application expertise across the production and further processing of man-made fibers. The key is to turn that knowledge into tailored solutions together with our customers.” Customer proximity will therefore be a key priority for Sielaff. articles.o: Karl Mayer expands fashion possibilities with TM Weft
articles.s: Karl Mayer will showcase the versatility of its TM Weft warp knitting technology at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026 in Shanghai, presenting a new collection of WovenLike fabrics alongside technical upgrades designed to expand the machine’s capabilities in fashion and apparel production. articles.x: Karl Mayer will showcase the versatility of its TM Weft warp knitting technology at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026 in Shanghai, presenting a new collection of WovenLike fabrics alongside technical upgrades designed to expand the machine’s capabilities in fashion and apparel production. Developed at the company’s Textile Innovation Center in Obertshausen, the collection demonstrates how warp knitting with weft insertion can produce fabrics with the appearance and characteristics of woven textiles while retaining the manufacturing efficiency and performance advantages of warp knitting. WovenLike warp knits combine the aesthetics of woven fabrics with properties such as ease of care, freedom of movement and crease resistance. According to Karl Mayer, the production process also offers environmental advantages over conventional weaving, particularly through reduced finishing requirements and associated wastewater treatment. While two- and three-bar tricot machines can produce WovenLike fabrics, the TM Weft is particularly suited to processing challenging materials, including effect yarns, linen and acetate fibres. The new collection comprises two contrasting fabric ranges, illustrating the machine’s flexibility across different fashion applications, from dense, textured autumn and winter fabrics to exceptionally lightweight chiffon-style materials. Dense fabric. © Karl Mayer The first range focuses on structured fabrics with sophisticated surface effects, combining warmth, comfort and distinctive aesthetics. articles.o: HKRITA sharpens focus on commercialisation
articles.s: The Hong Kong Research Institute of Textiles and Apparel (HKRITA) is strengthening its focus on bringing textile innovations to commercial scale, as it marks its 20th anniversary with new initiatives to expand industry collaboration. Speaking at the institute’s recent Innovation and Technology Sympo
articles.x: The Hong Kong Research Institute of Textiles and Apparel (HKRITA) is strengthening its focus on bringing textile innovations to commercial scale, as it marks its 20th anniversary with new initiatives to expand industry collaboration. Speaking at the institute’s recent Innovation and Technology Symposium 2026 in Hong Kong, CEO Jake Koh said the emphasis was increasingly on translating research into technologies that could be adopted commercially. “The true test of innovation begins when technology moves beyond the laboratory and into industry,” he said. “Today HKRITA measures success not only by how well a technology performs, but by how far it can go and the impact it can create.” A central element of this approach is the continued development of HKRITA’s Green Machine technology, designed to separate polyester and cotton from blended textile waste for subsequent recovery and recycling. Koh said the institute was working to refine the technology’s business model and accelerate its industrial deployment, reflecting the wider challenge facing textile recycling developers of moving beyond successful technical demonstrations to commercially viable operations. HKRITA has also opened an office in Shanghai this year to strengthen links with textile manufacturers, research institutions and technology partners in mainland China, particularly in the Yangtze River Delta. Chairman Teresa Yang said the expansion would support cross-regional research and accelerate the development of projects involving partners from different industries. The symposium also saw HKRITA sign a memorandum of understanding with Hong Kong’s Ocean Park Corporation to explore collaboration. articles.o: President stresses improved textile education to reduce reliance on foreign experts
articles.s: President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Sunday stressed the need to improve textile education and research to produce internationally competitive engineers and specialists and reduce the sector’s dependence on foreign experts. He made the remarks when a seven-member delegation led by Bangladesh Uni
articles.x: President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Sunday stressed the need to improve textile education and research to produce internationally competitive engineers and specialists and reduce the sector’s dependence on foreign experts. He made the remarks when a seven-member delegation led by Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Julhas Uddin paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban. MP from a reserved seat for women and BUTEX alumna Sanjida Islam were also present. Describing textiles as one of the country’s major economic sectors, the president emphasized the need to ensure suitable employment opportunities at home and abroad for textile graduates. This would help make proper use of the country’s skilled human resources while earning foreign currency, he said. The president also underscored the need to increase domestic cotton production to meet the raw material requirements of the textile industry. He called for taking initiatives to encourage farmers, explore ways to reduce production costs and strengthen coordination between the agriculture and textile sectors. He further stressed the need for more research into extracting fibers from natural sources, including jute, pineapple leaves and banana plants, alongside the development of synthetic yarn. During the meeting, the delegation briefed the president on BUTEX’s contributions to the development of the country’s textile and readymade garment industries, as well as its academic and research activities. They also highlighted several issues requiring attention, including infrastructure development, establishing modern laboratories, recruiting additional staff, creating a separate BCS (Textile) cadre, increasing budgetary allocations, and allocating land in Purbachal, Dhaka, for a second campus

Since acquiring Nomex from DuPont in April 2026, in a transaction valued at $1.8 billion, Arclin has focused on investing in capacity, reliability and long-term growth to meet increasing customer demand. The company is delivering record volume in 2026 and anticipates continued supply growth in 2027. “When we bought the Nomex business, we committed to investing in its future,” said Arclin CEO Bradley Bolduc. “Expanding production in Asturias will strengthen our global manufacturing network and help ensure we can continue supporting customers as demand grows across the aerospace, electrical infrastructure, defence and transportation markets.” The Asturias facility has been a cornerstone of the Nomex manufacturing network since 1993. Through this investment, the site will add Nomex nonwovens production capabilities and become one of four production facilities in Arclin’s global Nomex manufacturing network. articles.t: 방글라데시 직물 검사 기술로 Global Change Award 수상
articles.o: Bangladeshi fabric inspection technology earns Global Change Award
articles.s: Bangladeshi technology startup threadBridge has received the H&M Foundation’s Global Change Award 2026 for its AI-powered smart glasses, designed to help fabric inspectors detect defects in real time before fabric is cut. Co-founded by Md Ridwan Hossain and Mohammad Maaz, the startup received the aw
articles.x: Bangladeshi technology startup threadBridge has received the H&M Foundation’s Global Change Award 2026 for its AI-powered smart glasses, designed to help fabric inspectors detect defects in real time before fabric is cut. Co-founded by Md Ridwan Hossain and Mohammad Maaz, the startup received the award at Stockholm City Hall on 22 October. Hossain accepted the award, often called the “Nobel Prize of Fashion”, on behalf of the team, with Maaz alongside him, according to the press release. The venue hosts the Nobel Prize banquet each December. threadBridge was the only Bangladeshi company among this year’s 10 winners, alongside innovators from India, the United States, Sweden, the United Kingdom, France and Tanzania. The recognition highlights Bangladesh’s growing role in developing technology for the global textile industry. Long known as a major clothing manufacturing hub, the country is also gaining recognition for locally designed and built solutions that improve how those clothes are made. “Accepting this award in Stockholm, I was thinking of the workers on our factory floors,” said Hossain. “This recognition belongs to them, and to every young engineer in Bangladesh who wants to solve problems at home.” threadBridge’s smart glasses help inspectors identify fabric defects before cutting, allowing manufacturers to address quality issues earlier and reduce avoidable waste. According to the company, around 90% of fabric in many factories reaches the cutting stage without inspection. Defects discovered later can waste material, energy, and money. Alongside the glasses, threadBridge has developed a high-speed fabric inspection module that can be fitted to inspection machines factories already use. The company is piloting the module with garment manufacturers in Bangladesh

articles.t: 새로운 Woolmark 조사에서 소비자들은 천연 섬유를 선호합니다
articles.o: Consumers favour natural fibres in new Woolmark survey
articles.s: More than eight in ten consumers prefer natural fibres to synthetics when price, style and fit are equal, according to new Ipsos research commissioned by Woolmark across the USA, France, Germany, Italy and China. The survey found that an average of 82% of consumers across the five markets preferred
articles.x: More than eight in ten consumers prefer natural fibres to synthetics when price, style and fit are equal, according to new Ipsos research commissioned by Woolmark across the USA, France, Germany, Italy and China. The survey found that an average of 82% of consumers across the five markets preferred natural fibres, while 67% said they would be willing to pay more for clothing made mainly from them. Merino wool was preferred to polyester in every market surveyed, with an average of 65% of respondents favouring the natural fibre. The findings coincide with growing interest in wool, with worldwide Google search interest in Merino wool more than doubling over the past five years. The research also highlights the importance of transparency and verification, with 71% of respondents considering independent certification of fibre content and quality important. “Consumers want to know what a garment is made from, what that means in everyday use and whether the claims can be trusted,” said Woolmark managing director Bryan Fry. “That puts fibre, and the evidence behind it, back at the centre of the conversation.” For more than 60 years, Woolmark has supported research, testing, education and certification to provide evidence of wool’s quality and performance. Its new Natural Intelligence report examines Merino wool’s thermal comfort, moisture and odour management, durability and next-to-skin comfort. It includes findings from four years of research with North Carolina State University demonstrating how 100% Merino wool base layers help maintain a more stable next-to-skin microclimate during stop-start activity. The research also supports Woolmark’s new global brand campaign, Return to Real , which aims to reinforce the performance benefits of Merino wool through scientific evidence

articles.o: 블랙야크, 내마모성 2배 높인 ‘다이아퓨즈 다운재킷’
articles.s: 블랙야크가 일반 필라멘트 원단보다 내마모성이 2배 높은 ‘퍼텍스 다이아몬드 퓨즈(Pertex Diamond Fuse)’ 소재를 적용한 ‘다이아퓨즈 다운재킷 시리즈’를 출시했다.퍼텍스 다이아몬드 퓨즈는 다이아몬드 형태의 단면을 가진 필라멘트가 촘촘하게 맞물린 소재다. 블랙야크에 따르면 가벼우면서 긁힘과 마모에 강하고 은은한 광택이 특징이다. 여기에 퀼팅 디자인을 적용해 제품별로 차이를 뒀다.신제품은 ‘다이아퓨즈 다운재킷’, ‘다이아퓨즈 후디 다운재킷’, ‘다이아퓨즈 크롭 다운재킷’, ‘다이아퓨즈 라이트 다운재킷’ 4종이다.대표 제품인

articles.o: The vital signs of yarn feeding
articles.s: Memminger-IRO, a Vandewiele company, highlighted the importance of precision yarn feeding and tension control in modern knitting technology, at the recent The Loop – Chapter One: Medical Textiles (7-8 October 2026, at Groz-Beckert in Albstadt, Germany), demonstrating how advanced electronic systems
articles.x: Memminger-IRO, a Vandewiele company, highlighted the importance of precision yarn feeding and tension control in modern knitting technology, at the recent The Loop – Chapter One: Medical Textiles (7-8 October 2026, at Groz-Beckert in Albstadt, Germany ) , demonstrating how advanced electronic systems can improve fabric quality, production consistency and process reliability. In a technical presentation entitled The Vital Signs of Yarn Feeding – Precision in Tension Control , the German company’s Bennet Weisbach outlined developments in its EFS electronic yarn feeding technology, focusing on accurate tension regulation, high-speed responsiveness and integration with knitting machine control systems. The presentation explored four essential functions of yarn feeding systems: measuring, calibrating, controlling and stabilising yarn tension. Together, these functions provide the foundation for consistent yarn delivery, particularly as knitting machines operate at increasingly high speeds and process a wider variety of yarn types. At the heart of the technology is a continuous millisecond-based control loop, which regulates yarn tension through a relationship between measured tension and motor speed. Individual settings allow manufacturers to establish working tension, relaxation tension and recuperation tension according to the requirements of the knitting process. Calibration is another important element, with temperature-based calibration during the power-on sequence and time-based calibration during operation helping to maintain measurement accuracy. Memminger also emphasised the importance of adapting tension control to different yarn characteristics.
